title: Abstract C043: Sociodemographic predictors of knowledge of the HPV-cancer link and awareness of the HPV vaccine
abstract: Abstract Background: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) causes nearly all cervical cancers and contributes to several other malignancies. Although effective primary prevention strategies exist, disparities in HPV-related knowledge and awareness may contribute to inequities in vaccine uptake and cancer prevention. This study examined sociodemographic and geographic factors associated with HPV awareness, knowledge of the HPV-cervical cancer link, and awareness of the HPV vaccine among US adults. Methods: Data were analyzed from the 2022 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS 6), a nationally representative survey of US adults. Three separate survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine factors associated with 1) having heard of HPV, 2) knowledge of the HPV-cervical cancer link, and 3) having heard of the HPV vaccine. Models used jackknife replicate weights and adjusted for relevant sociodemographic factors. Complete case analysis with listwise deletion was used for each model. Results: In adjusted analyses, younger age was associated with HPV awareness, with adults aged 18–34 (OR=8.34, 95% CI 4.82–14.44) and 35–49 (OR=7.14, 95% CI 4.34–11.74) having higher odds than adults aged 75+. Compared to those with a college degree or higher, those with less than a high school degree had lower odds of HPV awareness (OR = 0.38, 95% CI 0.19-0.77). Women were more likely than men to report HPV awareness (OR=1.55, 95% CI 1.12–2.14). Lower awareness was observed among non-Hispanic Black (OR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.36-0.82), Hispanic (OR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.67), and non-Hispanic Asian (OR = 0.30, 95% CI 0.17-0.52) respondents compared to non-Hispanic White adults. For knowledge of the HPV-cervical cancer link, women (OR=1.55, 95% CI 1.12–2.14) and respondents aged 18-34 (OR 3.04, 95% CI 1.84-5.02) and 35-49 (OR = 3.26 95% CI 2.07-5.12) as well as those who ever had cancer (OR=1.69, 95% CI 1.20–2.39) had higher odds of correct identification. For HPV vaccine awareness, younger age was associated with awareness, with adults aged 18–34 (OR=5.98, 95% CI 3.89–9.18) and 35–49 (OR=5.72, 95% CI 3.73–8.75) showing higher odds than adults aged 75+. Women were more likely to be aware of the HPV vaccine (OR=3.01, 95% CI 2.38–3.81). Lower education (OR = 0.31, 95% CI 0.16-0.57) and lower income (OR = 0.45, 95% CI 0.30-0.67) were associated with reduced vaccine awareness, and cancer history increased awareness (OR=1.52, 95% CI 1.17–1.98). Rural residence and Appalachian status were not independently associated with any HPV knowledge outcomes after adjustment. Conclusions: HPV awareness and knowledge are strongly patterned by age, education, income, gender, and race/ethnicity. Rural residence and Appalachian status were not independently associated with HPV awareness, HPV-cervical cancer link, or vaccine awareness. Findings support the need for targeted health education and communication strategies to improve HPV-related awareness among men, older adults, and populations with lower educational attainment or income. Citation Format: Rachel A. Sociodemographic predictors of knowledge of the HPV-cancer link and awareness of the HPV vaccine [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr C043.

title: Clinical, Cytological, and Virological Factors Associated with Histological Severity and Recurrence in Vaginal Intraepithelial Neoplasia: A Retrospective Observational Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN) is a rare HPV-related condition with heterogeneous behavior and a relevant recurrence risk. Factors associated with severity and recurrence remain incompletely defined. OBJECTIVE: To explore clinical, cytological, virological, and colposcopic features associated with high-grade VAIN and recurrence. METHODS: This retrospective study included 42 women with histologically confirmed VAIN at a tertiary center between January 2020 and January 2026. All underwent vaginal cytology, high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) genotyping, colposcopy, and biopsy. Histology was classified as VAIN1 or VAIN2-3. Recurrence was defined as a histologically confirmed lesion after treatment and documented disease-free assessment. Associations were assessed using bivariate and exact analyses. RESULTS: VAIN2-3 was diagnosed in 31 women (73.8%). Among HR-HPV-positive women, HPV16-related infection was more frequent in VAIN2-3 than VAIN1 (65.4% vs 18.2%; OR 8.50, 95% CI 1.27-91.56; p = 0.013). Cytology was associated with histological grade (p = 0.024); all women with HSIL/ASC-H had VAIN2-3, although sensitivity was limited. Over a median follow-up of 24 months, eight women (19.0%) recurred after a median of 11.5 months. HPV16-related infection was more frequent with recurrence (75.0% vs 38.2%; OR 4.85, 95% CI 0.70-54.01; p = 0.112), but the evidence was not definitive. HPV16-only infection showed borderline evidence of association (p = 0.050), while no clear outcome pattern emerged for multiple-genotype infection. No other significant associations with recurrence were observed. CONCLUSION: HPV16-related infection was associated with high-grade histology among HR-HPV-positive women, while its prognostic relevance for recurrence remains uncertain. The limited sensitivity of cytology underscores the value of multimodal assessment. These exploratory signals warrant prospective validation.

title: Abstract B007: HPV genotype and YES1 oncogene alterations in cervical squamous cell carcinoma: A multi-cohort TCGA analysis
abstract: Abstract Background: YES1 is a Src-family tyrosine kinase implicated in oncogenic signaling in several squamous cell carcinomas, but its relationship to human papillomavirus (HPV) genotype in cervical cancer has not been characterized. We tested whether YES1 alteration frequency differs between the two most common high-risk HPV genotypes, HPV16 and HPV18. Methods: HPV genotype data for 178 core-set TCGA cervical cancer samples were obtained from the original TCGA cervical cancer publication. YES1 alteration data (amplification, mutation, and mRNA expression status) were independently obtained from three cBioPortal studies representing distinct reprocessings of this same TCGA sample collection: PanCancer Atlas, GDC-harmonized, and Firehose Legacy. Samples were merged by patient identifier and stratified by HPV16 versus HPV18 status. YES1 alteration frequency was compared between groups using two-tailed Fisher's exact tests, performed independently in each cohort. Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to assist with data merging, statistical scripting, and text drafting for this abstract; all analyses and results were independently reviewed and verified by the authors. Results: In the PanCancer Atlas cohort (n=92 HPV16, 26 HPV18), any YES1 alteration occurred in 13.0% of HPV16 versus 15.4% of HPV18 samples (p=0.75); high expression (z≥2) occurred in 4.3% versus 7.7% (p=0.61). In the GDC cohort (n=103 HPV16, 27 HPV18), any alteration occurred in 7.8% versus 3.7% (p=0.68); high expression occurred in 3.9% versus 3.7% (p=1.00). In the Firehose Legacy cohort (n=102 HPV16, 27 HPV18), any alteration occurred in 12.7% versus 14.8% (p=0.75); high expression occurred in 5.9% versus 7.4% (p=0.67). None of the six comparisons reached statistical significance. YES1 amplification, though rare, occurred exclusively in HPV16-positive samples in all three cohorts (2/92, 1/103, and 3/102, respectively), with zero amplification events in any HPV18 sample. Conclusions: Across three independently processed TCGA cervical cancer cohorts, no significant association was found between HPV16/HPV18 genotype and YES1 alteration frequency or expression. The consistent, HPV16-restricted pattern of rare YES1 amplification across all three cohorts may warrant further investigation with larger cohorts or functional validation. AI disclosure: Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to assist in drafting portions of this abstract's text; all content was reviewed, verified, and approved by the authors. Citation Format: Suleiman Kawu. HPV genotype and YES1 oncogene alterations in cervical squamous cell carcinoma: A multi-cohort TCGA analysis [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr B007.

source_records.title: Abstract B007: HPV genotype and YES1 oncogene alterations in cervical squamous cell carcinoma: A multi-cohort TCGA analysis
source_records.abstract: Abstract Background: YES1 is a Src-family tyrosine kinase implicated in oncogenic signaling in several squamous cell carcinomas, but its relationship to human papillomavirus (HPV) genotype in cervical cancer has not been characterized. We tested whether YES1 alteration frequency differs between the two most common high-risk HPV genotypes, HPV16 and HPV18. Methods: HPV genotype data for 178 core-set TCGA cervical cancer samples were obtained from the original TCGA cervical cancer publication. YES1 alteration data (amplification, mutation, and mRNA expression status) were independently obtained from three cBioPortal studies representing distinct reprocessings of this same TCGA sample collection: PanCancer Atlas, GDC-harmonized, and Firehose Legacy. Samples were merged by patient identifier and stratified by HPV16 versus HPV18 status. YES1 alteration frequency was compared between groups using two-tailed Fisher's exact tests, performed independently in each cohort. Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to assist with data merging, statistical scripting, and text drafting for this abstract; all analyses and results were independently reviewed and verified by the authors. Results: In the PanCancer Atlas cohort (n=92 HPV16, 26 HPV18), any YES1 alteration occurred in 13.0% of HPV16 versus 15.4% of HPV18 samples (p=0.75); high expression (z≥2) occurred in 4.3% versus 7.7% (p=0.61). In the GDC cohort (n=103 HPV16, 27 HPV18), any alteration occurred in 7.8% versus 3.7% (p=0.68); high expression occurred in 3.9% versus 3.7% (p=1.00). In the Firehose Legacy cohort (n=102 HPV16, 27 HPV18), any alteration occurred in 12.7% versus 14.8% (p=0.75); high expression occurred in 5.9% versus 7.4% (p=0.67). None of the six comparisons reached statistical significance. YES1 amplification, though rare, occurred exclusively in HPV16-positive samples in all three cohorts (2/92, 1/103, and 3/102, respectively), with zero amplification events in any HPV18 sample. Conclusions: Across three independently processed TCGA cervical cancer cohorts, no significant association was found between HPV16/HPV18 genotype and YES1 alteration frequency or expression. The consistent, HPV16-restricted pattern of rare YES1 amplification across all three cohorts may warrant further investigation with larger cohorts or functional validation. AI disclosure: Generative AI (Claude, Anthropic) was used to assist in drafting portions of this abstract's text; all content was reviewed, verified, and approved by the authors. title: Abstract A025: A pilot HPV self sampling intervention for cervical cancer screening among African American and African-born Black women
abstract: Abstract Background: Multifaceted barriers contribute to low cervical cancer screening rates among African Americans and African-born Black women. Human Papillomavirus (HPV) self-sampling is an approach with potential to help overcome barriers to cervical screening among under-screened women. HPV self-sampling can increase compliance with cervical cancer screening recommendations among African Americans and African-born Black women, but few community-based interventions have been developed to increase HPV self-sampling among these populations. This pilot study tested the efficacy and acceptability of the ‘Health is Wealth’ intervention among African American and African-born Black women. Methods: Sixty women needing cervical cancer screening based on the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force guidelines were recruited from the community. All participants were offered HPV self-sampling kits with instructions along with a one-time cervical cancer education session delivered by a peer educator over Zoom. Participants completed surveys at baseline, post-intervention (FU1), and at 6-month post-intervention (FU2). Data were collected on HPV knowledge, HPV testing knowledge, cervical cancer screening self-efficacy, cervical cancer knowledge, and cervical cancer risk. Repeated measures mixed modeling assessed changes in outcome variables over time. Results: Participants’ mean age was 36.1 years (SD = 5.9), and the HPV kit return rate was 71%. HPV knowledge and HPV testing knowledge scores significantly increased immediately post-intervention and remained elevated FU2 compared to baseline. Cervical cancer knowledge scores significantly increased from baseline to FU1 and significantly decreased at FU2. Similarly, cervical cancer risk scores significantly increased from baseline to FU1 and then decreased from FU1 to FU2. Cervical cancer self-efficacy scores did not change significantly over time. Conclusion: The high rate of return of HPV self-sampling kits supports feasibility and acceptability, positioning this approach as a practical and culturally responsive and sensitive alternative to clinic-based screening. Receiving the intervention was associated with significant short-term improvement in all variables except self-efficacy. Public health initiatives aimed at reducing cervical cancer screening disparities should consider integrating self-sampling into routine screening programs particularly for hard-to-reach populations. title: Shared-Antigen Cancer Vaccines Keep Falling Short.
abstract: BioNTech's HPV16 mRNA vaccine BNT113 failed to significantly delay progression of head and neck cancer in a phase II/III trial, the latest in a string of near-misses for off-the-shelf, shared-antigen cancer vaccines that reliably generate T cells but have struggled to improve patient outcomes. Researchers argue the vaccines themselves are working, and that success will depend on testing them in the right patients and settings and judging them by overall survival rather than tumor progression.

title: Within-host HPV–immune dynamics with epithelial turnover and downstream cervical disease burden: invasion, Hopf bifurcation, and intervention modelling
abstract: Abstract We formulate a deterministic within-host model for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, epithelial renewal, cellular immunity, precancerous epithelial burden, and downstream cervical-cancer burden. Susceptible, infected, and precancerous epithelial states share a normalised tissue-capacity constraint, while cancer is represented as a downstream pro-gression/removal compartment rather than an autonomous tumour-growth subsystem. This keeps the long-term disease module deliberately simple and avoids introducing an unsupported malignant-establishment threshold. We prove positivity and boundedness, identify the infection-free, epithelial-depleted infected-boundary, and positive coexistence equilibria, and derive an HPV invasion threshold that includes both infected-cell division and viral-load-mediated infection. Because cancer does not feed back into the epithelial–viral–lesion–immune subsystem, local oscillatory stability is governed by a five-dimensional core, while the cancer direction is automatically stable for positive removal. For an explicitly illustrative, non-calibrated benchmark, numerical continuation gives a simple Hopf point at μV ≈ 0.08722, with nonzero transversality and negative first Lyapunov coefficient under the stated convention. Long integrations confirm a stable periodic attractor on the unstable side of the crossing, although convergence is exceptionally slow. We also derive Pontryagin necessary conditions for therapeutic immune stimulation, screen-linked lesion treatment, and cancer therapy. The benchmark is intended for mathematical demonstration only; quantitative biological calibration, particularly of epithelial proliferation and immune/viral parameters, remains necessary before clinical interpretation.

title: The role of community pharmacists in updating the vaccination schedule: a descriptive analysis of vaccination data in the greater Paris Region, 2022-2024
abstract: Abstract Background: Community pharmacists in France have been authorized to prescribe and administer influenzae vaccines since 2019, and of all vaccines on the immunization schedule for individuals aged 11 years and older in August 2023. A few studies have explored patients’ and pharmacists’ perceptions of vaccination in community pharmacies, but their contribution to vaccination schedule adherence under routine conditions remains limited in France. The aim of this study was to evaluate the implementation of pharmacy-based vaccination in the greater Paris Region (Île-de-France (IDF) region), France. Methods: We analysed the vaccines (excluding COVID-19 vaccines) prescribed and administered by healthcare professionals in the greater Paris Region (Ile de France, IDF) over a three-year period (2022-2024), using the database of the National Health Data System (Système National des Données de Santé, SNDS). Results: The total number of vaccine doses administered by pharmacists in the IDF Region increased from 896,663 in 2022 to 1,802,705 in 2024 (101% increase), mainly due to influenza vaccination (n= 880,845 in 2022 and n= 1,280,744 in 2024). Among vaccines for which recommendations were updated during the study period, the number of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine doses administered in community pharmacies increased from 431 in 2022 to 51,105 in 2024, and 5,089 doses of respiratory syncytial virus vaccine were administered in 2024, compared to none before 2024. In 2024, 67,435 pneumococcal vaccine doses were administered in community pharmacies, of which 2.6% were prescribed by pharmacists. In 2024, 5% of doses (n=27,997/521 961 doses, excluding influenza vaccines) administrated were prescribed by pharmacist. The majority (68%, n= 18,936/27,997) were combined diphtheria-tetanus-poliomyelitis vaccines with reduced-antigen acellular pertussis (dTaP/IPV), while herpes zoster vaccines represented the smallest share (0.1%, n= 41). Of all combined dTaP-IPV vaccines prescribed by pharmacists in 2024 – a year marked by a pertussis epidemic– 95% included the pertussis component. Conclusion: The study evaluates pharmacy-based vaccination activity in the IDF Region, according to prescribing and administration practices. The encouraging rates of prescribing and administration by pharmacists for vaccines with recently updated recommendations highlight pharmacist’s frontline role in infection prevention and their responsiveness to new recommendations and epidemic situations.

title: Development of a Behavioral Intervention, Increasing HPV Vaccine Uptake-Delivered in Dental Settings (HPV Vaccine Uptake-DDS) .
abstract: We developed a behavioral intervention designed to address barriers faced by dental practitioners promoting the Human Papillomavirus vaccine to eligible patients. Guided by the Behavior Change Wheel; our approach included a rapid literature review and interviews with dental practitioners to identify and understand these barriers. We then applied the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behavior model and the Theoretical Domains Framework to identify and specify draft intervention functions which were mapped to the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy. These functions target key barriers, in particular, lack of knowledge of HPV/HPV vaccine, lack of self-efficacy to promote the HPV vaccine, and fears about potential negative consequences of doing so. To assess initial acceptability of our intervention and inform refinements, we surveyed parents/guardians of vaccine-eligible patients under age 18, as well as vaccine-eligible patients aged 18-26. We also conducted stakeholder conversations and timed the delivery of the intervention. The final HPV Vaccine Uptake-DDS intervention includes didactic training, scripted text and tailored messages embedded within a clinical decision support (CDS) tool designed for chairside use, and performance feedback to practitioners. Preliminary findings suggest the intervention is time-efficient and acceptable to practitioners and patients/parents/guardians. Although funding for our real-world efficacy trial has been cut, we are committed to securing support for such a trial. If HPV Vaccine Uptake-DDS is demonstrated to be effective, it could lead to greater HPV vaccine uptake thereby contributing to the prevention of oropharyngeal cancers.

title: Baseline and early changes in serum proteomic profiles predict anti-tumor activity in patients with advanced HPV-associated malignancies treated with novel combination immunotherapy
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with advanced human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancies who do not respond to immune checkpoint blockade have limited treatment options. Combination immunotherapy consisting of an HPV16 therapeutic peptide cancer vaccine (PDS0101) to initiate an immune response, a tumor-targeting IL-12 immunocytokine (PDS01ADC) to potentiate that response, and a bifunctional agent providing dual blockade of programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1) and transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) (bintrafusp alfa) to reduce immunosuppression has demonstrated promising clinical activity in a prior report of a clinical trial in patients with advanced HPV16 + –associated malignancies (NCT04287868). Here, we provide updated clinical results from that trial and identify immune correlates of clinical response. Methods We performed a comprehensive survey of the peripheral immunome from 38 patients with HPV16 + tumors, and built machine-learning models using a survey of serum proteomic data to predict which patients would derive clinical benefit and improved overall survival from treatment. Results Models incorporating baseline levels of IL- 6 and heme oxygenase 1, alone or with an early change in granzyme B, effectively predicted clinical benefit and duration of overall survival. We also identified a persistent skewing of increased peripheral CD8 + T cells to myeloid cell ratios in patients who benefit from treatment. Moreover, there was a positive association between monocyte and myeloid derived suppressor cell frequencies with serum concentrations of inhibitory biomarkers, providing biological rationale of the serum-based prediction models. Conclusions Although retrospective, these data demonstrate outcome prediction in patients with HPV-associated malignancies using readily quantifiable molecular correlates from minimally invasive sampling of peripheral blood prior to therapy or early in the regimen and thus provide the rationale for prospective validation in future clinical studies.
journal: Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research

title: Abstract C176: An informatics-driven framework for precision cervical cancer prevention in conflict-affected Northern Ethiopia: Linking HPV prevention gaps, traditional postpartum vaginal fumigation (Weyba Tis), and health system disruptions
abstract: Abstract Background: Cervical cancer remains a major cause of illness and death among women in Ethiopia. Data from Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital showed that cervical cancer was the second most commonly diagnosed malignancy, accounting for 12.3% of 4,229 cancer cases recorded between 2017 and 2025. Nearly two-thirds of patients came from conflict-affected areas, highlighting geographic disparities and the effects of prolonged disruption to vaccination, screening, diagnosis, and treatment services. Traditional postpartum vaginal fumigation, known locally as Weyba Tis or Kerbe, remains common in parts of Northern Ethiopia. However, its relationship with cervical cancer prevention and healthcare-seeking behavior has not been systematically studied. Objective: To develop an informatics-driven framework for examining how conflict-related health system disruption, gaps in human papillomavirus (HPV) prevention, and traditional postpartum vaginal fumigation may collectively contribute to cervical cancer disparities in Northern Ethiopia. Methods: We propose a mixed-methods implementation science study integrating hospital cancer registry data, OpenMRS-compatible electronic health records, geographic information systems, and community survey data. Quantitative analyses will examine associations among HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening, conflict exposure, access to care, diagnostic delay, stage at presentation, and reported use of traditional postpartum practices. Spatial and predictive models will identify areas with low screening participation and delayed diagnosis. Qualitative interviews with women, community members, traditional practitioners, and healthcare professionals will explore cultural beliefs, postpartum practices, healthcare-seeking patterns, and barriers to HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening. Expected Results: The framework is expected to identify geographic, behavioral, sociocultural, and health system factors associated with gaps in HPV prevention, screening, and timely diagnosis in conflict-affected communities. Integrating clinical, geographic, and community data may help identify women at greatest risk, clarify how health system disruption contributes to missed prevention opportunities, and generate testable hypotheses about the role of Weyba Tis in reproductive health decisions and care-seeking. Possible biological effects on the cervical or vaginal microenvironment will require separate mechanistic and microbiome studies. Conclusions: This framework brings together cancer surveillance, health informatics, implementation science, spatial epidemiology, and culturally grounded reproductive health research. The findings may support culturally responsive interventions, strengthen HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening, improve cancer surveillance, and guide precision public health strategies in Ethiopia and other conflict-affected settings. title: Rapidly Progressive Buschke-Löwenstein Tumor Managed With Wide Local Excision and Healing by Secondary Intention: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Buschke-Löwenstein tumor (BLT) is a rare, locally aggressive anogenital tumor associated predominantly with low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. BLT is classically described as a slow-growing lesion predominantly affecting middle-aged men who are immunocompromised; cases of rapid progression are rarely reported. We present the case of a 23-year-old male with a progressively enlarging perianal mass over 1 year that was accompanied by rectal pain and intermittent bleeding. He reported prior unprotected heterosexual intercourse, though serologic testing for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B/C was negative. CT imaging revealed a fungating lesion entirely distal to the dentate line without evidence of internal extension. Subsequently, the patient underwent wide local excision with electrocautery fulguration, and the wound was managed with healing by secondary intention. Histopathology revealed clear margins around a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) without high-grade dysplasia or carcinoma; in situ hybridization (ISH) confirmed HPV types 6 and 11, without detection of high-risk HPV. A review of the literature on BLT epidemiology, histopathology, differential diagnosis, and management is presented. This case illustrates that BLT can progress rapidly in young, immunocompetent individuals and highlights that healing by secondary intention following wide local excision is a viable option in appropriately selected cases.

source_records.abstract: Buschke-Löwenstein tumor (BLT) is a rare, locally aggressive anogenital tumor associated predominantly with low-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11. title: Mechanisms by which programmed cell death mediates immune evasion and antitumour immunity in oropharyngeal cancer
abstract: The development and treatment response of oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) are jointly shaped by tumour cell-intrinsic features and the tumour immune microenvironment (TIME). Programmed cell death (PCD) determines tumour cell fate and modulates antitumour immunity by altering immunogenicity, the release of immunostimulatory signals and immune-cell function. Dysregulated PCD can enable tumour cells to evade immune recognition, establish an immunosuppressive state and alter the response to immunotherapy. Here, the roles of PCD in regulating immunity in oropharyngeal cancer (OPC) are reviewed, with emphasis on understanding at the molecular level how processes involved in apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and autophagy contribute to either immune evasion or antitumor immunity, with consideration given to emerging pathways involving necroptosis and cuproptosis. The immunological effects of cell death are thought to be context-dependent rather than predetermined by the mode of execution. Immunologically silent death can dampen these processes, reducing the immunogenicity of tumors, impairing antigen processing and presentation, and limiting T cell recognition; conversely, immunogenic cell death (ICD) can drive functional immunological responses through the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), improved antigen presentation, as well as adaptive immunity activation. Next, differences between human papillomavirus (HPV)-positive and HPV-negative OPSCC are discussed regarding PCD, TIME remodeling, immune checkpoint activation, and treatment resistance, as well as their translational relevance to precision immunotherapy, radiosensitization, and chemosensitization via subgroup-based combination therapy. Given the limited OPSCC-specific evidence for several emerging PCD pathways, related findings from head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) studies are discussed to provide mechanistic context. Together, these insights provide a framework for understanding immune evasion in OPC and for developing PCD-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Abstract IA049: Genomic diversity, sociomicrobiome determinants, and immunomodulatory role of fannyhessea in HPV, dysplasia, and cervical cancer among Arizona cohorts
abstract: Abstract While the emerging sociomicrobiome framework explains how lived experiences and social conditions shape microbial ecosystems and influence disease risk, the direct causal contributions of specific cervicovaginal bacteria, such as Gardnerella, Fannyhessea, and Sneathia, to HPV persistence and cervical carcinogenesis remain unclear. Further, higher rates of cervical cancer (CC) disproportionately affect Hispanic and Native American women with persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, with cervicovaginal microbiome being an underrecognized contributing factor in addition to broader structural determinants of health. Fannyhessea species are key bacteria linked to bacterial vaginosis (BV), HPV persistence, and progression to CC. We hypothesized that social determinants influence Fannyhessea carriage and that genomic diversity within Fannyhessea drives distinct pathogenicity and host immune responses that contribute to HPV persistence and progression to CC. Thus, we utilized clinical, genomic, and in vitro studies to decipher role of Fannyhessea species in HPV infection and CC. The study analyzed two Arizona-based patient cohorts, comparing individuals with cervical pathology, diagnosed HPV infection, and patients undergoing routine annual woman’s exams. We analyzed 16S rRNA microbiome, immunoproteome, and HPV genotyping data from these patients' cervicovaginal samples and assessed clinical and sociodemographic associations. We also infected 3D human cervical epithelial cell models with representatives of three Fannyhessea species to assess epithelial-derived immune responses and performed comparative genomic analyses of Fannyhessea genomes. Fannyhessea vaginae was the most prevalent species in both cohorts, with an average of 50%, followed by Fannyhessea species type 2 (21%) and then Fannyhessea massiliense (20%). Integrating sociomicrobiome factors revealed that high parity, increased household size, and no higher education background were associated with Fannyhessea carriage, cervicovaginal dysbiosis, and HPV status. Native American and Hispanic patients had higher Fannyhessea carriage compared to White and non-Hispanic counterparts. Fannyhessea carriage correlated with elevated vaginal pH and increased species richness. In a clinical cohort, Fannyhessea were associated with elevated levels of proinflammatory, immune checkpoint, and cancer-associated immune markers. In vitro analyses revealed similar epithelial-derived immune profiles among the three Fannyhessea species. Genomic analyses identified species-specific protein families related to antibiotic resistance, potential barrier disruption, virulence, and niche adaptation. Clinical and laboratory studies determined that Fannyhessea act as emerging cervicovaginal pathogens, triggering inflammation and oxidative stress that can advance CC. This work highlights how social determinants shape microbial risk factors and underscores the potential of targeted, microbiome-based interventions to reduce CC disparities among high-risk and underserved populations. Citation Format: Nicole Jimenez, Pawel Laniewski, Melissa Herbst-Kralovetz. Genomic diversity, sociomicrobiome determinants, and immunomodulatory role of fannyhessea in HPV, dysplasia, and cervical cancer among Arizona cohorts [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr IA049.

title: Divergent Effects of Trichomonas vaginalis on Cervical Cancer Cells HPV-positive and HPV-negative: Interplay with Purinergic Signaling.
abstract: Trichomonas vaginalis is the protozoan that causes trichomoniasis, the most common non-viral sexually transmitted infection in the world. Recently, studies have highlighted the possible association between T. vaginalis and the development of cervical cancer, as well as co-infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), suggesting a role of the protozoan in oncogenesis. In the cervical cancer context, the purinergic signaling influences immunosuppression and angiogenesis, while high concentrations of adenosine can induce cell death. vaginalis uptakes adenosine for survival as well it takes advantage in its immunomodulatory effects. Thus, the presence of T. vaginalis could influence cell survival, modulating the tumor microenvironment. Our study demonstrated that, in ex vivo models, T. vaginalis increased cell proliferation, immune infiltrate, and vascularization. Meanwhile, in in vitro 2D cell culture models, T. vaginalis combined with purinergic signaling differentially affects the viability of HPV-positive (SiHa) and HPV-negative (C33A) cervical cancer cell lines, with significant impact in the cell line without HPV. The ATP and adenosine signaling did not affect the cytotoxicity exerted by conditioned medium against both cell lines. vaginalis reduced the IL-6 production and E6 oncogene expression by SiHa cells. the Ki-67 gene expression was modulated by the parasite and ATP/adenosine metabolism, highlighting the plasticity of the purinergic signaling combined with the parasite. These findings indicate that T. vaginalis exerts cytotoxicity and modulation of pathways relevant to the tumor microenvironment, influencing cell death, inflammation, and tissue remodeling processes, and shed light to further studies on the interactions between T. vaginalis and host cells.

title: A novel HPV mRNA vaccine candidate: immunogenicity and definition of immune correlates of protection
abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV), the major cause of cervical cancer, continues to be associated with an increasing number of diagnosed cases despite the availability of licensed vaccines such as CervarixTM and GARDASIL ® . In addition, cervical cancer incidence remains especially high in low- and middle-income countries, while vaccine coverage remains low due to high costs and instability in supply. We developed a novel HPV vaccine candidate using mRNA platform and to propose immune correlates of protection (CoP) for efficacy evaluation. A protection threshold was established based on GARDASIL ® 9, and the corresponding antibody titers were determined. These antibody titers were used as Reference for the immunogenicity analysis of the generated HPV16 mRNA. As a result, the vaccine was shown to induce a sufficiently significant level of protective efficacy. Furthermore, based on the immunogenicity data obtained from GARDASIL ® 9 and HPV16 mRNA, the minimum antibody titers required for protection were determined, thereby defining CoP for HPV vaccine. Additionally, HPV16 mRNA induced cellular immune responses associated with CD4- and CD8-specific cytokine secretion, suggesting potential protective mechanism in which cellular immunity complements humoral immunity. This study proposes an objective evaluation framework for comparing and analyzing HPV vaccine efficacy across different vaccine platforms.

title: Abstract A134: Prevalence of non-vaccine targeted oncogenic oral and genital HPV types among U.S. adults
abstract: Abstract Introduction: More than 200 human papillomavirus (HPV) types have been identified, but only 12 are carcinogenic. The 9-valent HPV vaccine targets seven carcinogenic types (HPV16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58), including HPV16/18, which account for most HPV-associated cancers. However, HPV35, 39, 51, 56, and 59 are not covered by current vaccines and are less well characterized. Data on these non-vaccine-targeted (NVT) types among U.S. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of adults aged ≥18 years from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2013-2016 of oral, vaginal, and penile HPV. We estimated survey-weighted type-specific HPV prevalence by race/ethnicity and used Poisson regression to calculate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs), adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, lifetime cigarette smoking, number of lifetime sexual partners, and HPV vaccination status. Results: Oral HPV prevalence was low overall, with HPV16 the most frequently detected type (0.89%), followed by HPV59 (0.53%), HPV51 (0.39%), HPV35 (0.20%), HPV56 (0.19%), HPV39 (0.14%), and HPV18 (0.09%). Non-Hispanic White (NHW) participants had the highest prevalence of oral HPV16 (1.08%) and HPV51 (0.48%), while Non-Hispanic Black (NHB) participants had the highest prevalence of HPV18 (0.25%), HPV35 (0.64%), HPV56 (0.45%), and HPV59 (0.87%). Males had a higher prevalence of all oral types. Genital HPV prevalence was highest for HPV51 (4.21%), followed by HPV16 (3.41%), HPV59 (2.94%), HPV39 (2.61%), HPV35 (1.65%), and HPV18 and 56 (1.5% each). NHW participants had the highest prevalence of genital HPV16 (3.76%); NHB participants had the highest prevalence of HPV18 (2.69%), HPV35 (4.34%), HPV51 (5.45%), HPV56 (1.80%), and HPV59 (4.41%). Males had a higher prevalence of all genital types, except HPV56. Dual oral-genital infections were rare, occurring most frequently in HPV59 (0.24%), followed by HPV16 and 51 (0.14% each). Dual infections were most common in HPV16, 18, 35, and 59 for NHB participants, in HPV39 for other racial/ethnic groups, and in HPV51 for NHW participants. NHB participants (aPR 1.91, 95% CI 1.10-3.30) and vaccinated individuals (aPR 2.08, 95% CI 1.01-4.30) had a significantly higher prevalence of any NVT oncogenic HPV compared with NHW participants and unvaccinated individuals, respectively. Increasing lifetime number of sexual partners was independently associated with a higher prevalence of NVT oncogenic HPV, whereas associations with sex and lifetime cigarette smoking were not statistically significant. Conclusion: NVT oncogenic HPV genotypes were prevalent among U.S. adults, with type distribution and site varying by race/ethnicity. The association between HPV vaccination and NVT HPV warrants confirmation in longitudinal studies. Further investigation of their contribution to HPV-associated malignancies may inform the development of expanded vaccines targeting additional oncogenic HPV types. Citation Format: Morgan C. title: Improving HPV vaccine knowledge and acceptance through educational intervention: a quasi-experimental study of healthcare students in Saudi Arabia
abstract: Introduction Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major cause of cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal cancers worldwide. Despite the availability of a highly effective vaccine, HPV vaccine uptake remains notably low in Saudi Arabia. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of an educational intervention in improving HPV vaccine knowledge and reducing hesitancy among healthcare students in Saudi Arabia. Methods A quasi-experimental one-group pre-test/post-test design was conducted at King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from May 2023 to March 2024. A total of 355 healthcare students completed a validated questionnaire before a structured one-hour educational session addressing HPV infection, associated cancers, and vaccination, and 324 post-session questionnaires were returned. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and logistic regression. Results Following the intervention, correct responses to knowledge items increased from 12–22% pre-intervention to 45–80% post-intervention (all p < 0.0001), while vaccine hesitancy declined from 63.7 to 28.7% ( p < 0.0001). Male gender was independently associated with higher hesitancy, whereas prior awareness of the vaccine was associated with lower hesitancy. Lack of information, the leading reason for hesitancy pre-intervention, declined markedly post-intervention. Conclusion These findings highlight the effectiveness of targeted educational programs in improving HPV vaccine awareness and acceptance among healthcare students in Saudi Arabia, supporting their integration into healthcare curricula.

title: Abstract C181: HPV vaccination uptake among age-eligible adults in a high-risk clinic-based population in Puerto Rico
abstract: Abstract Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection can cause several cancers including, anal, cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, and oropharyngeal. The primary strategy for preventing HPV-related cancers is HPV vaccination, which is recommended for individuals aged 9 through 26 years. Additionally, HPV vaccination is approved for individuals up to age 45 based on shared clinical decision-making with their healthcare provider. Although immunologic response of the HPV vaccination is greatest at younger ages, some adults may still benefit from vaccination. Information on HPV vaccination uptake among age-eligible adults at high-risk of HPV-related cancers in Puerto Rico remains limited. Objective: To assess factors associated with HPV vaccination uptake among age-eligible patients attending the Anal Neoplasia Clinic of the University of Puerto Rico Comprehensive Cancer Center (ANC-UPRCCC). Methods: Data from baseline visits of adults aged 18-45 years attending the ANC-UPRCCC were analyzed (N=577). At the baseline visit, participants completed a physician-administered questionnaire that collected information on sociodemographic, clinical, and lifestyles characteristics. HPV vaccination status was defined as receipt of at least one dose of the HPV vaccine. Pearson chi-square and logistic regression models were used to evaluate factors associated with HPV vaccine uptake. Results: Most participants were men (78.8%), aged 27-45 years (84.2%), and living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (65.8%). HPV vaccine uptake was 27.2%, with 60.0% of vaccinated individuals reporting completion of the 3-dose series. Age, sex, smoking status, alcohol consumption, HIV status, health insurance status, relationship status, lifetime number of sexual partners, and history of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) were significantly associated with HPV vaccine uptake in the bivariate analysis (p<0.05). Both people living with HIV (PLWH) (aOR=0.38; 95% CI: 0.22-0.63) and adults aged 27-45 years (aOR=0.34; 95% CI: 0.19-0.61) had lower odds of HPV vaccination compared with HIV-negative individuals and adults aged 18-26, respectively. Participants with ≥26 lifetime sexual partners (aOR=2.63; 95% CI: 1.21-5.72) and those who currently consumed alcohol (aOR=3.23; 95% CI: 1.28-8.15) had higher odds of HPV vaccination than their respective counterparts. Conclusions: HPV vaccination uptake was suboptimal among age-eligible adults attending the ANC-UPRCCC, with notably lower uptake among PLWH and those aged 27-45. These findings highlight gaps in Puerto Rico’s current vaccination efforts. Increasing awareness on adult HPV vaccine eligibility, strengthening provider recommendations, and implementing culturally appropriate educational strategies may improve HPV vaccine uptake and reduce the incidence of HPV-related cancers in Puerto Rico. Citation Format: Michelle Torrico, Jeslie M. Ramos-Cartagena, Cristina Muñoz, Maribel Tirado, Miriam Matos, Keimari Méndez, Ana P. HPV vaccination uptake among age-eligible adults in a high-risk clinic-based population in Puerto Rico [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr C181.

title: Abstract B150: A community health assessment to inform cervical cancer prevention and reduce disparities in the Tri-County region of Illinois
abstract: Abstract Background: Cervical cancer screening and Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) vaccination have led to the decline in incidence and mortality from cervical cancer in the United States; however, geographic disparities persist. The mostly rural, semi-urban Tri-county region of Illinois (IL) experiences a higher burden of cervical cancer with an incidence rate that exceeds that of the state (11.6 vs 7.4 per 100,000 women respectively). Peoria, Tazewell, and Woodford counties make up this region and are defined by both metropolitan and rural characteristics as well as racial and socioeconomic diversity. To understand cervical disparities in these three counties, we employed a cross-sectional community health assessment which evaluated barriers to care, awareness of cervical cancer risk factors and prevention, as well as completion of preventive screening and HPV vaccination. Methods: Participants were recruited through health care clinics, cancer screening initiatives, community outreach events, and digital platforms. Surveys were self-administered and were completed online or in-person. Participants aged 18-20 were surveyed about knowledge and attitudes about screening guidelines, HPV vaccination, cervical cancer risk, and preferences for educational programming. Additionally, participants aged 21+ were asked about past screening and barriers to screening completion. Descriptive statistics were computed to assess community needs and inform targeted interventions. Results: Of the 180 participants, 53.2% self-identified as Black and 31.1% self-identified as White. Most participants had at least a high school education or higher (93.8%) and were insured (76%). Among those eligible for screening, 52.8% reported having a past cervical cancer screening test, while 37.4% reported never completing screening. Although most participants reported awareness of screening (75%) and HPV vaccination (67%), knowledge gaps remained. Only 21.3% of participants believed that screening was necessary if symptoms were present, and 31.7% were unfamiliar with current screening guidelines. These knowledge gaps were accompanied by barriers to preventive services such as transportation (16.7%), cost (15%), time (13%), and fear of the test results (10%). Overall, 71.7% participants identified a need for community education around cervical cancer prevention, with a preference for in-person programming delivered in the community or by health care providers. Conclusions: Cervical cancer screening rates among participants are significantly lower than national and state averages. Community-identified barriers to screening and the need for more education highlight specific targets that may improve uptake of screening and vaccination in this region. These findings will help guide the development of future interventions and policies which aim address cervical cancer disparities. Funding: This research was made possible with funding provided by The Community Health Advocacy initiative through University of Illinois Chicago and OSF HealthCare. title: Abstract A116: The vaginal microbiome, precancerous cervical lesions, and racial and ethnic disparities: A scoping review
abstract: Abstract Objective: To synthesize evidence linking the vaginal microbiome with precancerous cervical lesions and cervical cancer and to examine how race and ethnicity have been incorporated into this literature. Background: Vaginal microbial dysbiosis has been associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) persistence and cervical carcinogenesis. Although racial and ethnic disparities in cervical cancer incidence and outcomes are well documented, it remains unclear whether differences in vaginal microbial composition contribute to these disparities or whether race and ethnicity have been adequately evaluated in microbiome studies. Methods: We conducted a scoping review using the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis and reported findings according to PRISMA-ScR. The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework before data collection. Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, SciELO, Global Index Medicus, and the Cochrane Library were searched. Eligible studies evaluated the vaginal microbiome in relation to precancerous cervical lesions, or cervical cancer and reported participant race, ethnicity, or geographic population. Two reviewers independently screened records and charted study design, population characteristics, microbiome methods, cervical outcomes, and the treatment of race and ethnicity in study analyses. Narrative and systematic reviews were included if they met the predefined inclusion criteria (i.e., they reported on precancerous cervical lesions, such as CIN 1–3 or cervical dysplasia, or progression to cervical cancer). These reviews were synthesized separately as secondary evidence and were not counted as primary studies. Results: Thirty-five studies published between 2006 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria, with sample sizes ranging from 34 to 18,466 participants. Studies were conducted in North America (n=10), Latin America (n=6), Europe (n=5), Africa (n=4), Asia (n=9), and multicenter study (n=1). Most studies were cross-sectional (n=13) or observational (n=8), and cervical outcome measures varied substantially. Race and ethnicity, were primarily described rather than evaluated as potential modifiers of the association between the vaginal microbiome and precancerous cervical lesions. 13 studies analyzed race and ethnicity, 6 compared racial or ethnic groups, 4 adjusted for race or ethnicity, and 1 tested effect modification, highlighting the limited evaluation of racial and ethnic differences. Conclusion: Vaginal microbiome dysbiosis appears to be associated with cervical disease progression, but evidence regarding racial and ethnic variation remains fragmented and methodologically heterogeneous. Longitudinal, prospective, multicenter studies using standardized microbiome methods and adequately powered, diverse populations are needed to clarify temporality and determine whether microbial signatures can improve cervical cancer risk prediction and prevention without reinforcing race as a biological proxy. title: An exploratory Case Report: integrated genomic and transcriptomic profiling of a spontaneous facial tumor in the endangered Milu deer (Elaphurus davidianus)
abstract: The Milu deer ( Elaphurus davidianus ), also known as Père David's deer, has experienced severe population bottlenecks. While infectious diseases are closely monitored, baseline data on sporadic non-communicable diseases, such as neoplasia, remain scarce for wildlife disease surveillance. To date, the molecular mechanisms driving spontaneous tumorigenesis in this species remain uncharacterized. This study provides the first integrated characterization of a single facial tumor in the Milu deer, combining histopathological analysis, whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). Histopathological analysis confirmed that the tumor is an epithelial neoplasm exhibiting significant mesenchymal features, indicative of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). RNA-seq differential expression analysis identified 6,537 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), while WGS revealed 114 high-confidence, tumor-specific non-synonymous somatic mutations. Functional enrichment analysis demonstrated that oncogenesis in this specific specimen is potentially driven by dysregulated cell cycle, cytoskeletal reorganization, and metabolic reprogramming mediated by PI3K-Akt and mTOR signaling. Notably, the human papillomavirus (HPV) infection pathway emerged as significantly enriched among the DEGs. We emphasize that this enrichment does not provide evidence of viral involvement, as no direct viral detection was performed; rather, it exclusively reflects the severe dysregulation of highly conserved host cellular networks implicatedin cell cycle, apoptosis, and immune regulation. By integrating mutational and transcriptomic data, we prioritized ten putative tumor-associated genes, including LGALS3, DMBT1, CHAF1A, GON4L , and SIRPA , which are linked to metastasis, immunosuppression, and proliferation. This case study provides the first integrated molecular profile of a facial tumor in the Milu deer, offering critical insights for health management of this endangered species and establishing a novel framework for comparative oncology that will inform future clinical diagnoses of neoplasms in this population.

title: Expanding HPV Vaccine Among Young Adults: A Preventive Step Against Gynecological Cancers
abstract: Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a major preventable cause of cervical and other HPV-related cancers. Despite the proven effectiveness of HPV vaccination, knowledge gaps and misconceptions continue to limit vaccine uptake among young adults. This study aimed to evaluate HPV awareness, attitudes and beliefs regarding HPV testing, and vaccination-related health beliefs among young adults and to examine the relationships among these constructs. Methods: This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted with 313 young adults aged 18–25 years in Turkey. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using a Personal Information Form, the HPV Awareness and Concern Scale, the HPV Testing Attitudes and Beliefs Scale, and the Health Belief Model Scale for HPV Infection and Vaccination. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), Pearson correlation analyses, and post hoc tests, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Although most participants were aware of HPV and its association with cervical cancer, substantial knowledge gaps remained regarding the appropriate timing and purpose of HPV vaccination. Most participants recognized that sexual activity was not a prerequisite for vaccination, whereas awareness of HPV-related cancers other than cervical cancer remained limited. HPV awareness was positively correlated with attitudes and beliefs regarding HPV testing (r = 0.239, p < 0.01) and vaccination-related health beliefs (r = 0.337, p < 0.01). Similarly, HPV testing attitudes and beliefs were positively associated with vaccination-related health beliefs (r = 0.228, p < 0.01). These findings indicate that, despite relatively high HPV awareness, important misconceptions and knowledge gaps regarding HPV vaccination persist among young adults. Conclusions: Targeted educational interventions, evidence-based social media campaigns, and healthcare professional-led counselling strategies may contribute to improving vaccine acceptance and strengthening HPV-related cancer prevention efforts.

title: Longitudinal melanonychia as a presenting sign of nail unit squamous cell carcinoma: A case series and narrative review
abstract: Background: Nail unit squamous cell carcinoma (nSCC) presenting as longitudinal melanonychia is underrecognized, particularly among patients with skin of color (SOC). This review identifies patient, tumor, and human papillomavirus (HPV) characteristics. Summary: A review from peer-reviewed articles plus five institutional cases yielded 59 total cases. The majority (69.6%) were male, with a median age of 53 years. Among those with known Fitzpatrick Skin Type or race, 86.9% had SOC. Fingernails accounted for 87.7% of tumors. Longitudinal melanonychia was the only finding in 23.7% of cases, while hyperkeratosis, onychodystrophy, and verrucous changes were reported in 30.5%, 18.6%, and 15.3% of cases, respectively. The lateral nailfold was involved in 80.6% of cases. Most (81.4%) tumors were in situ at diagnosis. When performed, HPV testing was positive in 76.0% of cases, with high‐risk types (including HPV 16, 56, 58, and 59) predominating (76.9%). Key Messages: nSCC should be considered in the differential of longitudinal melanonychia, especially in patients with SOC over age 40 and a history of HPV infection presenting with lateral nailfold involvement, hyperkeratosis, onychodystrophy, or verrucous changes. Recognizing these findings may reduce diagnostic delay and allow earlier, tissue‐sparing treatment.

title: Abstract C157: The impact of HPV status and history of other STIs on cervical lesion severity in a cohort of pregnant women living in Puerto Rico
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Human papillomavirus (HPV), a known causative agent of cervical cancer, has a lifetime prevalence of 80%. Pregnancy-related immune changes and other sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as chlamydia, gonorrhea, herpes simplex virus 2, human immunodeficiency virus, and bacterial vaginosis may influence HPV persistence and cervical dysplasia. To the best of our knowledge, no study has examined these predictors together in pregnant women living in Puerto Rico. We hypothesized that high-risk HPV (hr-HPV) genotypes and STI history would be associated with more severe cervical lesions in this population. Methods: This retrospective sub-analysis included 126 pregnant women recruited at two clinics located in San Juan, Puerto Rico between 2016 and 2024. Patients completed a questionnaire self-reporting history of STIs and other relevant risk factors. Cervicovaginal samples were HPV typed using SPF10-LiPA25 or Atila AmpFire systems, and cytology was evaluated using a liquid-based method. Colposcopy was indicated for patients with cytology ≥ ASC-US and/or a positive HPV result; cervical lesion grade was determined by clinician consensus using cytology and/or pathology results. Associations between HPV status, history of other STIs, and cervical lesion severity were assessed using Fisher's exact test and binary/ordinal logistic regression, adjusting for age and pregnancy trimester. Results: HPV prevalence was 59.5% with HPV-52 and HPV-16 being the most prevalent genotypes. HPV-positive women had 5.61 times the odds of abnormal cervical lesions compared to HPV-negative women (95% CI: 2.41-13.06). HPV-16/18 positive women showed 6.73 times the odds of severe lesions compared to HPV-negative women (95% CI: 2.44-18.54). Past medical history of STIs was 38.1%, with chlamydia the most reported STI (17.5%). History of other STIs was not independently associated with lesion severity (adjusted OR=1.57, 95% CI: 0.65-3.79). Elevated vaginal pH was independently associated with increased lesion severity (OR=4.63, 95% CI: 1.71-12.51), and HPV vaccination was protective against high-grade cervical lesions (OR=0.26, 95% CI: 0.08-0.81). Discussion: HPV status, but not past medical history of STIs, independently predicted cervical lesion severity in our cohort of pregnant patients, with HPV-16/18 showing the strongest association. Elevated vaginal pH was independently associated with lesion severity, suggesting vaginal dysbiosis as an additional, modifiable risk factor. HPV vaccination showed a protective association against high-grade cervical lesions, reinforcing its role as a critical prevention strategy for reproductive-age and pregnant women. Conclusion: These findings address a key gap in the literature on HPV and cervical dysplasia in pregnant women in Puerto Rico and support incorporating HPV genotyping and vaginal pH assessment into cervical lesion screening during pregnancy, while reinforcing the value of HPV vaccination in reducing lesion risk. The impact of HPV status and history of other STIs on cervical lesion severity in a cohort of pregnant women living in Puerto Rico [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr C157.

title: Abstract A037: Expanding access to cervical cancer screening in Philadelphia: A novel HPV self-collection program
abstract: Abstract Background: The purpose of our pilot study is to evaluate the feasibility of same-day human papillomavirus (HPV) self-collection in a community setting that aims to reduce disparities in access to cervical cancer screening. Cervical cancer is preventable through HPV screening. HPV self-collection has been shown to decrease disparities in screening by overcoming financial, cultural, and logistical barriers to accessing clinician-collected HPV testing. However, optimal strategies for community-based self-collection outreach are incompletely understood. Methods: This pilot was performed in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania through the Abramson Cancer Center, University of Pennsylvania in partnership with local churches and community organizations. Individuals with a cervix ages 25-65 years who attended community health outreach events between June 2025-May 2026 were invited to participate in this IRB exempt study. Exclusion criteria were hysterectomy, immunocompromised status, pregnancy or childbirth in the past three months, and recent cervical screening or treatment. Eligible participants completed a self-administered questionnaire in REDCap assessing demographics, clinical history, and barriers to screening and received written and verbal instructions for using BD OnclarityTM self-collection kits. Individuals performed self-collection in a private bathroom before completing a post-collection questionnaire assessing their experience. Samples were genotyped and study investigators coordinated follow-up care per current guidelines. The primary outcome was feasibility of same-day HPV self-collection in a community setting. Secondary outcomes included HPV genotype results, diagnostic resolution, and individual perspectives on cervical cancer screening. Results: A total of 22 individuals met inclusion criteria and completed HPV self-collection. The median age was 52 years (range 33-65 years), the majority identified as Black (18/22, 81.8%), over half reported seeing a primary care physician (12/22, 54.5%) and had insurance coverage (16/22, 72.7%). Distance barriers, time and financial constraints, and lack of screening awareness were reported reasons for overdue cervical screening. Seven individuals testing HPV-positive (7/22, 31.8%), including two for HPV 16/18, were contacted by study investigators and navigated to appropriate follow-up care. Over half preferred self-collection (12/22, 54.5%) versus no preference and cited convenience, privacy, and ease of use as factors when choosing an HPV collection method. Conclusion: This novel pilot demonstrates the feasibility of same-day community-based HPV self-collection to expand cervical cancer screening access and reduce disparities. Although our small sample size limits generalizability, future efforts will focus on scaling the initiative through partnerships with community organizations and faith-based groups. Citation Format: Sarah A. Phillips, Gurbani Singh, Isabella An, Eniola Okon, Sejin Lee, Emily Verderame, Carmen E. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. title: Abstract IA050: Decoding the role of lifestyle and behavioral factors on the microbiome–metabolome axis in cervical cancer risk
abstract: Abstract Cervical cancer remains one of the most common cancers in women worldwide, with the human papillomavirus (HPV) being the identified etiological agent. Over the past decade, incidence rates among women in Puerto Rico have increased, potentially reflecting socioeconomic barriers that limit access to healthcare and contribute to lower screening rates. An essential component of cervical dysplasia is persistent HPV infections that progress to cervical lesions of low- and high-grade severity. Importantly, biological factors, including the cervicovaginal microbiome, may contribute to the progression of cervical dysplasia and subsequent cancer development. Specifically, the cervical microbiome can alter the metabolic environment through microbial-derived metabolites, providing a potential biological pathway linking microbiome-environment interactions with cancer development. Due to the limited understanding of the underlying metabolic pathways, our study evaluated the cervical microbiota-metabolome axis and other lifestyle markers in Hispanic women with HPV and cervical dysplasia living in Puerto Rico. This cohort of non-menopausal, reproductive-age women underwent bacterial identification by 16S rRNA sequencing, HPV genotyping, and untargeted metabolomics using Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry. Microbial assessment identified that women with high-severity lesions exhibited increased richness and pro-inflammatory taxa, including Prevotella spp., Sneathia, and Fusobacterium. Interestingly, oral-associated taxa were linked to metabolic processes involving several metabolites in the cervical microenvironment, including biogenic amines. Overall, oral-associated taxa emerged as potential predictors of metabolic variations across cervical progression. Our lab continues to evaluate the role of high-risk behavior in cervical cancer progression and is also interested in understanding the dynamics between fungal and bacterial communities. Our findings highlight the potential role that sexual behaviors, such as oral sex, and lifestyle play in facilitating microbial translocation that may contribute to cervical disease. Funding for this study was provided by the NIH Center for Collaborative Research in Minority Health and Health Disparities (RCMI) 2U54MD007600, the Puerto Rico Clinical and Translational Research Consortium (PRCTRC) U54MD007587, and the Puerto Rico IDeA Network Biomedical Research Excellence (PR-INBRE) 5P20GM103475-17. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the University of Puerto Rico-Medical Sciences Campus (Protocol #1050114, Streamline #2290033153), with biosafety approval under protocol #94620. Citation Format: Natalie M. Meléndez-Vázquez, Filipa Godoy-Vitorino. Decoding the role of lifestyle and behavioral factors on the microbiome–metabolome axis in cervical cancer risk [abstract]. source_records.title: Abstract IA050: Decoding the role of lifestyle and behavioral factors on the microbiome–metabolome axis in cervical cancer risk
source_records.abstract: Abstract Cervical cancer remains one of the most common cancers in women worldwide, with the human papillomavirus (HPV) being the identified etiological agent. Over the past decade, incidence rates among women in Puerto Rico have increased, potentially reflecting socioeconomic barriers that limit access to healthcare and contribute to lower screening rates. An essential component of cervical dysplasia is persistent HPV infections that progress to cervical lesions of low- and high-grade severity. Importantly, biological factors, including the cervicovaginal microbiome, may contribute to the progression of cervical dysplasia and subsequent cancer development. Specifically, the cervical microbiome can alter the metabolic environment through microbial-derived metabolites, providing a potential biological pathway linking microbiome-environment interactions with cancer development. Due to the limited understanding of the underlying metabolic pathways, our study evaluated the cervical microbiota-metabolome axis and other lifestyle markers in Hispanic women with HPV and cervical dysplasia living in Puerto Rico. title: Abstract A053: Pre-contact attrition in the Sacred Womb Initiative: EHR-based screening limitations in cervical cancer disparities research
abstract: Abstract Background: Electronic health record (EHR)-based identification can facilitate recruitment to prospective studies, but little is known about where potential participants are lost before contact. We characterized pre-contact attrition in the Sacred Womb (SW) Initiative, a prospective cohort examining psychological stress, the vaginal microbiome, human papillomavirus, and cervical lesion outcomes among Latina, non-Latina Black, and non-Latina White women referred for colposcopy after abnormal cervical screening. Methods: From August 11, 2025, through July 13, 2026, potentially eligible women aged 21–65 years were identified at VCU Health using a standardized Epic anatomic pathology report filtered for selected abnormal cervical cytology results. Medical records were reviewed for cytology, colposcopy recommendation and timing, prior screening history, pregnancy, HIV status, hysterectomy, race and ethnicity, and other protocol criteria. Screening outcomes were recorded in REDCap. Eligibility was assessed according to the protocol version in effect at screening; a prior abnormal cervical screening result was an exclusion only during part of the study period. Each woman who did not advance was assigned one mutually exclusive primary reason. Descriptive statistics summarized pre-contact attrition and advancement to recruitment. Results: Among 176 women reviewed, 25 (14.2%) advanced to direct screening and 151 (85.8%) did not. Protocol-defined, clinical, or study-population criteria accounted for 80 non-advancements (53.0%): nonqualifying cytology (n=42), a prior abnormal cervical screening result excluded under the applicable protocol version (n=16), pregnancy (n=13), not meeting the study’s prespecified race and ethnicity eligibility criteria (n=6), HIV-positive status (n=2), and prior hysterectomy (n=1). Potentially modifiable scheduling or timing losses accounted for 37 (24.5%): identification fewer than 16 days before colposcopy (n=23), no scheduled colposcopy despite recommendation (n=13), and canceled colposcopy (n=1). Documentation-limited losses accounted for 34 (22.5%): no documented colposcopy recommendation (n=33) and race or ethnicity not listed in the EHR (n=1). Descriptive advancement rates were 17.4% among Latina women (4/23), 14.9% among Black women (11/74), and 11.9% among White women (7/59). Among the remaining three women who advanced, race or ethnicity was unknown for two and one declined to answer. Conclusions: Only one in seven EHR-identified women advanced to direct recruitment. Most non-advancement occurred because women identified by the initial EHR report did not meet full eligibility criteria after medical-record review. However, nearly one-quarter was related to colposcopy scheduling or timing, identifying a potentially modifiable point of recruitment loss. Earlier identification, integration with colposcopy scheduling workflows, and more precise EHR algorithms may improve recruitment efficiency and support equitable enrollment in cervical cancer disparities research. Generative AI was used to assist with language editing. Citation Format: Bahira Ahmed, Bianca D. Owens, Myrlene Jeudy, Jessica G. LaRose, Jerome Strauss III, Gregory A. Bae-Jump, Katherine Y. title: The cervicovaginal microbiome as a candidate correlate and potential predictor of HPV clearance and treatment response after HSIL therapy: a scoping review
abstract: Background Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) infection causes virtually all high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) and cervical cancer, but only a minority progress, implicating host and microenvironmental cofactors. The cervicovaginal microbiome (CVM), particularly Lactobacillus-dominated communities, may influence hrHPV persistence, clearance, and response to HSIL treatment. Objective To map evidence linking the CVM with hrHPV clearance and outcomes after HSIL treatment, including loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) and conization, using PRISMA-ScR and Arksey and O’Malley frameworks. Methods Literature on cervicovaginal microbiota, community state types (CSTs), HPV natural history, HSIL/CIN treatment, probiotics, microbiome-directed interventions, and predictive biomarkers was systematically searched and narratively synthesized using a Population-Concept-Context framework. Results Sixty-six sources were charted. Lactobacillus crispatus -dominated communities (CST-I) were associated with hrHPV clearance and favorable post-treatment outcomes, whereas CST-IV, bacterial vaginosis, and increased alpha-diversity were associated with hrHPV persistence, greater HSIL severity, and treatment failure. Proposed mechanisms include lactic acid-mediated pH regulation, D-lactic acid signaling, and modulation of viral oncoproteins and immune responses. Excision altered the CVM, with restoration of Lactobacillus dominance accompanying viral clearance. Microbial-signature machine-learning models showed promising but preliminary predictive performance. Oral and intravaginal probiotics showed inconsistent but generally favorable trends, with strongest evidence for intravaginal L. crispatus transplantation. Gut microbiome diversity may also influence chemoradiotherapy outcomes in invasive cervical cancer. Conclusion The CVM is a promising predictor of hrHPV clearance and HSIL treatment response. However, methodological heterogeneity, small cohorts, and limited prospective evidence restrict clinical translation. Large prospective studies and rigorously designed trials are needed to validate predictive signatures and determine whether microbiome profiling or targeted modulation can improve HSIL management and outcomes.

title: Abstract C169: Disparities in guideline-concordant breast and cervical cancer screening among Medicaid-insured female childhood cancer survivors: A report from the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Childhood cancer survivors are at increased risk for subsequent malignancies and require guideline-recommended cancer screening. Existing evidence relies largely on self-reported screening measures. This study used administrative Medicaid claims to evaluate rates of guideline-concordant breast and cervical cancer screening and identify disparities among female childhood cancer survivors. Methods: We used established linkage between the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS) and national Medicaid claims. Breast cancer screening-eligible CCSS survivors included 884 females who were aged ≥40 years and/or met Children's Oncology Group risk-based screening criteria (≥25 years of age and ≥8 years after chest radiation or total body irradiation), with continuous Medicaid coverage and no prior breast cancer. Cervical cancer screening-eligible CCSS survivors included 1,509 females aged ≥21 years, with continuous Medicaid coverage and no prior cervical cancer. Breast (mammogram or breast magnetic resonance imaging) and cervical (Pap smear or human papillomavirus testing) cancer screenings were identified using procedure and diagnosis codes in claims data. For each eligible person-year, survivors were classified as up to date with breast cancer screening if they had ≥1 screening claim during the current or preceding year (2-year look-back), and up to date with cervical cancer screening if they had ≥1 screening claim during the current or preceding two years (3-year look-back). Multivariable regressions examined factors associated with screening being up to date. Results: During 2014-2019, the proportion of eligible survivors who were up to date increased from 23.2% to 31.0% for breast cancer screening and from 32.9% to 37.0% for cervical cancer screening. For breast cancer screening, survivors aged 40-64 years were more likely to be up to date than those aged 25-39 years (OR=6.13, 95% CI=3.99-9.42), while survivors residing in the highest-poverty communities were less likely to be up to date than those in the lowest-poverty communities (OR=0.61, 95% CI=0.40-0.93). A different pattern emerged for cervical cancer screening, with survivors having severe or life-threatening chronic conditions being less likely to be up to date than those with mild or no chronic conditions (OR=0.76, 95% CI=0.62-0.93). Conclusions: Using administrative claims, we found that less than one-third of survivors received guideline-concordant breast and cervical cancer screening among Medicaid-insured childhood cancer survivors. Estimated screening rates were consistent with prior claims-based studies of the general Medicaid population but lower than those reported in some survey-based studies of childhood cancer survivors, potentially reflecting objective ascertainment with claims data, the socioeconomically vulnerable Medicaid population, or both. Factors associated with screening differed across screening modalities, suggesting the need for screening-specific strategies to improve secondary cancer prevention among childhood cancer survivors.
