title: Abstract B160: Willingness to perform HPV self-sampling among women living with HIV in Puerto Rico: Findings from the 2023–2024 Medical Monitoring Project
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Women living with HIV (WLWH) are at increased risk of persistent high-risk HPV infection and cervical cancer (CC) compared with women without HIV. Despite recommendations for routine CC screening, participation remains suboptimal because of systemic, financial, and psychosocial barriers. HPV self-sampling has emerged as a promising strategy to address these barriers by increasing privacy, autonomy, and convenience. However, willingness to use this screening approach among WLWH has not been well characterized. This study assessed willingness to perform HPV self-sampling and associated factors among Hispanic WLWH in Puerto Rico (PR). Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional secondary data analysis of 85 WLWH participating in the 2023-2024 cycles of the Medical Monitoring Project (MMP) in PR who completed the local survey. Willingness to perform HPV self-sampling was self-reported and categorized as willing (probably or willing) versus not willing (not sure, probably not, or definitely not). Prevalence estimates for HPV self-sampling willingness were calculated as weighted percentages with 95% confidence intervals (CI) by sociodemographic, social determinants of health, and lifestyle behaviors. Log-binomial regression models estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% CIs using Stata 19.0 survey procedures. Generative artificial intelligence was used solely to improve grammar and language. Results: Participants had a mean age of 54.8±14.3 years, and 73.1% reported a cervical Pap test within the past 3 years. Overall, 32.6% of WLWH were willing to perform HPV self-sampling. In unadjusted analyses, higher annual income and health literacy were significantly associated with greater willingness to perform HPV self-sampling; however, these associations were attenuated after adjustment. WLWH with annual income ≥ $20,000 (aPR=1.89, 95% CI: 0.99-3.58) and greater confidence completing health forms (aPR=2.11, 95% CI: 0.91-4.90) were more likely to report willingness to perform HPV self-sampling than their counterparts. Additionally, women covered by Medicaid, another public insurance program, or the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program (aPR=0.66,95% CI: 0.33-1.34), as well as those covered by Medicare (aPR=0.37, 95% CI: 0.10-1.38), were less likely to report willingness to perform HPV self-sampling than women with private insurance. The prevalence of willingness did not differ by education or alcohol use. Conclusion: Approximately one-third of WLWH in PR reported willingness to perform HPV self-sampling. Although willingness appeared to vary by socioeconomic factors, larger studies are needed to confirm these associations. As the first study to assess willingness to perform HPV self-sampling among WLWH in PR, these findings provide baseline evidence to inform future implementation studies evaluating HPV self-sampling as a strategy to increase CC screening participation among WLWH in PR. title: Changes in attitudes toward the HPV vaccine in Kenya
abstract: Globally, attitudes about vaccines and vaccination are changing rapidly, but few studies have examined within-person shifts over time. We use a longitudinal survey in Kenya to assess how respondents’ attitudes about the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine changed between 2022 and 2024. In 2022, we conducted a random digit-dialed phone survey of 1405 Kenyan parents/caregivers of girls age-eligible for the HPV vaccine; respondents were re-contacted in 2024, and 1093 people (78%) were successfully re-surveyed. Each survey included identical questions about HPV vaccine and vaccination attitudes (adapted from the Vaccine Hesitancy Scale-HPV). We estimate direction and degree of each person’s change in attitude, overall and by construct/question, and explore associations between these changes and respondent demographics, and baseline knowledge about HPV and HPV vaccination. Attitudes about the HPV vaccine changed substantially from 2022 to 2024. Although perceptions of the vaccine’s importance and effectiveness were relatively stable (only 25% of respondents reported any attitude change), there were significantly more changes among respondents with lower educational attainment and who were unemployed. Safety perceptions changed substantially over this period: two-thirds of respondents changed their beliefs around the vaccine’s side effects and riskiness. Approximately one-quarter of respondents developed a worse safety attitudes, while 18.9% of respondents improved their safety attitude. Among individuals with lower socioeconomic status, attitudes about following a clinician’s HPV vaccination recommendation and riskiness of the HPV vaccine significantly worsened over this period. We found that, in this population of Kenyan adults and over a two-year period, attitudes about the HPV vaccine have changed both positively and negatively. Targeted interventions may be needed, particularly with less socioeconomically-advantaged groups, to reinforce messages about the vaccine’s importance, effectiveness, and safety. Further research is needed about reasons for the large changes in safety perceptions, both toward more and less favorable views.

In 2022, we conducted a random digit-dialed phone survey of 1405 Kenyan parents/caregivers of girls age-eligible for the HPV vaccine; respondents were re-contacted in 2024, and 1093 people (78%) were successfully re-surveyed. Each survey included identical questions about HPV vaccine and vaccination attitudes (adapted from the Vaccine Hesitancy Scale-HPV). We estimate direction and degree of each person’s change in attitude, overall and by construct/question, and explore associations between these changes and respondent demographics, and baseline knowledge about HPV and HPV vaccination. Attitudes about the HPV vaccine changed substantially from 2022 to 2024. Although perceptions of the vaccine’s importance and effectiveness were relatively stable (only 25% of respondents reported any attitude change), there were significantly more changes among respondents with lower educational attainment and who were unemployed. Safety perceptions changed substantially over this period: two-thirds of respondents changed their beliefs around the vaccine’s side effects and riskiness. Approximately one-quarter of respondents developed a worse safety attitudes, while 18.9% of respondents improved their safety attitude. Among individuals with lower socioeconomic status, attitudes about following a clinician’s HPV vaccination recommendation and riskiness of the HPV vaccine significantly worsened over this period. We found that, in this population of Kenyan adults and over a two-year period, attitudes about the HPV vaccine have changed both positively and negatively. Targeted interventions may be needed, particularly with less socioeconomically-advantaged groups, to reinforce messages about the vaccine’s importance, effectiveness, and safety. Further research is needed about reasons for the large changes in safety perceptions, both toward more and less favorable views.

title: Cristazine inhibits HPV-positive cervical cancer cells via inducing caspase-dependent apoptosis
abstract: Objective: To determine whether cristazine inhibits HPV-positive cervical cancer cells and to elucidate its underlying mechanisms. Methods: HeLa cells were treated with varying concentrations of cristazine, and cell viability, intracellular ROS, apoptosis, and apoptosis-related gene and protein expression were assessed using WST-1, DCF-DA flow cytometry, Annexin V-FITC/PI staining, quantitative RT-PCR, and Western blotting. Additionally, CaSki and SiHa cells were evaluated in viability assays, with selected ROS and apoptosis measurements performed in CaSki cells. Results: After 24 h of treatment, cristazine reduced HeLa cell viability with an IC 50 of 0.223 μM and increased intracellular ROS and apoptotic populations. Caspase inhibition substantially restored viability and reduced apoptosis. Cristazine also increased TP53, CDKN1A, BAX, BCL2 , and CASP3 expression, and reduced HPV18 E6/E7 expression. Additionally, Western blotting showed upregulated p53, p21 and Bax/Bcl-2 ratio, and increased cleavage of caspases-3, -8, -9, and -12 and PARP after cristazine treatment. DAPI staining showed chromatin condensation, while wound healing assays demonstrated reduced wound closure following cristazine treatment. Conclusions: Cristazine suppresses cervical cancer cell growth via coordinated ROS-associated, p53-driven, and caspase-dependent apoptotic signaling, highlighting its potential as a marine-derived anticancer candidate that warrants further investigation.

title: Reanalysis of public bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomes identifies widespread tumor-normal dysregulation and a cross-layer cell-cycle signal in sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Background Sinonasal squamous cell carcinoma (SNSCC) is a rare malignancy affecting the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection identified as a critical etiological factor in a subset of cases. HPV-positive and HPV-negative SNSCC exhibit distinct clinical behaviors, with HPV-positive tumors generally demonstrating better prognosis and treatment response. However, the cellular composition and transcriptomic landscape of SNSCC tumor versus normal tissue remain incompletely characterized. Multi-layer transcriptomic reanalysis of publicly available single-nucleus and bulk RNA sequencing data provides an opportunity to systematically identify tumor-normal gene expression changes and nominate candidate biomarkers for prospective validation. Methods We reanalyzed publicly available single-nucleus RNA sequencing data (GSE277797: one healthy nasal mucosa library, HC1; one SNSCC tumor library, CA5) together with bulk RNA-seq data from 14 SNSCC and normal nasal mucosa samples (GSE278145), microarray data from five matched tumor-adjacent-normal pairs (GSE138809), and a 21-sample sinonasal cancer tumor-only context cohort (GSE118386). Following rigorous quality control, doublet detection, cell-type annotation using canonical markers, and program scoring, we integrated findings across data layers. Candidate genes were further assessed by in vitro experiments in two SNSCC cell lines (RPMI 2650 and Detroit 562) compared with normal bronchial epithelial BEAS-2B cells, using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) to evaluate mRNA expression levels (2 −ΔΔCT method, GAPDH reference) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to quantify secreted and intracellular protein concentrations. Results Single-nucleus analysis resolved 14,479 nuclei into 11 biological cell types, with the largest observed compositional shift being an increase in Epithelial cells (+44.7 percentage points) and a decrease in Secretory epithelial cells (−56.2 percentage points) in the tumor library relative to the healthy library. Bulk RNA-seq differential expression testing across 17,677 genes identified 5,732 genes at FDR <0.05, with cell-cycle genes showing the largest program-level shift (+1.727 standardized units). Cross-layer integration yielded a Spearman correlation of 0.543 between bulk fold-changes and single-nucleus pseudobulk shifts. Candidate genes including CD74, CCL5, IL32, and HLA-DRA showed concordant upregulation across data layers. In vitro qRT-PCR confirmed significant mRNA upregulation of CD74 (4.27-fold), CCL5 (3.15-fold), IL32 (3.68-fold), and HLA-DRA (3.82-fold) in RPMI 2650 cells compared to normal BEAS-2B cells (all p < 0.01), with elevated protein levels further corroborated by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Conclusion This multi-layer transcriptomic reanalysis of publicly available SNSCC datasets identifies consistent tumor-versus-normal dysregulation across single-nucleus and bulk platforms, and nominates CD74, CCL5, IL32, and HLA-DRA as candidate biomarkers warranting prospective clinical validation. These findings are exploratory and should be interpreted within the constraints of the available single-sample single-nucleus data.

title: Parental perceptions, information sources, and practices related to childhood immunization and HPV vaccine awareness in Saudi Arabia: an observational study
abstract: Background Parents’ perceptions, information sources, and household vaccination practices influence routine childhood immunization and may also shape responses to newer vaccines. We conducted an updated Saudi survey using an adapted instrument and included a human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine module to assess self-reported awareness and recommendation intention. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among parents in Saudi Arabia from June to July 2025. The Arabic questionnaire covered vaccination awareness and perceptions, information sources, parent-reported practices and experiences, with two HPV-specific items. Descriptive analyses used chi-square/Fisher’s exact tests. Multivariable binary logistic regression examined factors associated with HPV vaccine awareness, and an exploratory multinomial logistic regression examined HPV vaccine recommendation intention. Results A total of 513 parents were included. Self-reported general vaccine awareness was 96.9%. Routine vaccination uptake was 98.8%, and 90.6% reported completing recommended vaccinations. Awareness of national immunization programs was 57.9%, and 61.4% reported satisfaction with vaccination information in the media; 71.7% did not believe vaccination is harmful. Health workers were the most frequently selected source of vaccination information (60.0%). HPV vaccine awareness was 68.6%, and 52.4% would recommend HPV vaccination for their child, while 19.1% selected “I do not know.” In adjusted analysis, HPV vaccine awareness was higher among females (aOR 1.87; 95% CI 1.23–2.86), among parents in all other regions compared with the Southern region (aORs 2.02–3.38), among those reporting problems during vaccination (aOR 2.82; 95% CI 1.76–4.51), and among those expressing either a harmful or non-harmful view of vaccination compared with “I do not know.” In the exploratory multinomial analysis, HPV vaccine awareness was associated with a lower relative likelihood of responding “I do not know” rather than “Yes” to HPV vaccine recommendation intention (aRRR 0.07; 95% CI 0.04–0.13). title: The Role of Viral Pathogens in the Promotion of Epithelial–Mesenchymal Transition and Neoplastic Cell Invasion
abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a multistep process in which stationary, polarized epithelial cells lose cell-to-cell adhesion and acquire a mesenchymal phenotype with migratory and invasive properties. Migrating EMT cells express both epithelial and mesenchymal markers, an intermediate hybrid state that allows them to retain some epithelial traits for survival while gaining mobility. After migration and metastasis to a secondary tumor site, EMT cells revert to an epithelial-like state via a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) to establish new tumors. Cells undergoing EMT may also acquire cancer stem cell properties, leading to chemotherapy resistance and cancer recurrence. Accumulating evidence suggests that both oncogenic and non-oncogenic viruses can induce EMT. Among the oncogenic viruses, EMT has been reported in neoplastic cells infected with human papillomavirus, hepatitis B and C viruses, Epstein–Barr virus, and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. Non-oncogenic viruses, including human cytomegalovirus and human immunodeficiency virus, can also induce EMT in neoplastic cells. Furthermore, coinfection of neoplastic cells with two or more oncogenic viruses or oncogenic and non-oncogenic viruses may lead to synergistic and/or additive effects with respect to EMT induction. This review presents our current understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying virus-induced EMT and the role of this transition in promoting neoplastic disease.

title: How Peer Discussion of Cervical Cancer Screening Centers on the Exam: Topic Modeling and Network Analysis Study
abstract: Background: Cervical cancer is largely preventable, yet it caused about 604,000 new cases and 280,000 deaths worldwide in 2024. Fear can motivate or deter screening, and fear of cancer differs from fear of the exam itself. Online health communities record these concerns in users’ own words, which makes them a practical source of insight for screening programs.Objective: This study mapped the topics of cervical cancer screening discussion in peer online health communities, how those topics connect, and where negative emotion and fear concentrate.Methods: We analyzed 9851 posts and comments from 7 women’s health subreddits posted between August 1, 2025, and January 31, 2026. Latent Dirichlet allocation and the Analysis of Topic Model Networks procedure identified topics, clusters, and bridging topics. A transformer sentiment model classified each document as negative, neutral, or positive; we validated it, a second transformer model, and the VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner) lexicon against 2 coders’ consensus coding of 209 documents. We counted explicit fear terms by topic and their co-occurrence with procedure and disease terms.Results: The model yielded 13 substantive topics that formed 3 clusters (modularity 0.30): diagnostic information, the embodied experience of the exam, and personal narrative with peer support. Timing and bleeding, the least prevalent topic (3.5%), had the highest betweenness centrality (0.26) across network thresholds. The transformer model agreed with human coding more closely (macro F1=0.61) than VADER (macro F1=0.41), which labeled 40% of human-coded negative documents as positive. By the transformer model, 36.8% of documents were negative and 19.6% positive, and encouragement and support was the only topic with more positive than negative documents. Fear terms appeared in 3.5% of documents on human papillomavirus (HPV) and cancer risk, the lowest share of any topic, against 21.8% for pain and discomfort and 27.0% for accounts of clinical visits. Sentences expressing fear mentioned the procedure without the disease far more often than the reverse (559 vs 66). HPV and cancer risk connected to the exam-experience cluster only through access to care.Conclusions: In this discourse, fear attaches to the screening exam far more than to cervical cancer, and the topics that connect the conversation concern bleeding, pain, and getting an appointment. Screening communication may gain more from building confidence about the exam, through clear information on what to expect, pain management, and self-sampling options, than from further emphasis on cancer risk. Lexicon-based sentiment tools should be used with caution in health contexts, where words such as positive carry clinical meaning.

title: Augmented Reality Flipbook Innovation to Increase Self-Awareness for Cervical Cancer Early Detection Through HPV DNA Screening Among Women of Childbearing
abstract: Cervical cancer remains a health problem among women in low- and middle-income countries. Early detection through screening, including human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA testing, is a strategy. However, low knowledge and self-awareness regarding cervical cancer and HPV DNA screening remain barriers to screening utilization. Health education media are needed. This study aimed to develop an Augmented Reality-based flipbook to improve self-awareness in women of childbearing age. The study used the 4D model (Define, Design, Develop, and Disseminate). Validation involved material, media, and language experts, followed by a user test involving 15 women of childbearing age. The effectiveness test included 30 women of childbearing age using a one-group pretest-posttest design. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test. The AR-based flipbook showed high feasibility, with scores of 85.94% for material, 92.50% for media, and 98.07% for language experts, while the user test scored 90.78%. High self-awareness increased from 3.3% to 43.3%, while the low category decreased from 26.7% to 0%. The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test showed a significant difference in self-awareness before and after intervention (p = 0.004). The AR-based flipbook demonstrated high feasibility and potential as an educational medium for improving self-awareness of cervical cancer early detection in women of childbearing age.
journal: International Journal of Psychology and Health Science

title: Abstract C106: From natural compound to targeted therapy: Curcumin-loaded hydrogels for cervical cancer prevention and treatment
abstract: Abstract Cervical cancer remains the fourth most common cancer among women worldwide and disproportionately affects populations in low-resource settings where access to human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, routine screening, and treatment services is limited. Despite effective preventive measures, a woman dies from cervical cancer approximately every two minutes, highlighting the urgent need for affordable, accessible, and minimally invasive therapeutic strategies. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV is the primary driver of cervical cancer development, making interventions that target HPV-associated disease progression particularly important. Curcumin, possesses anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and antitumor properties. Previous studies have demonstrated its ability to inhibit cancer cell proliferation, induce apoptosis, and modulate immune responses associated with tumor progression. However, the clinical utility of curcumin has been limited by poor bioavailability and rapid degradation. To overcome these challenges, we propose the use of a fibrin-based hydrogel (FBH), a biocompatible and biodegradable delivery platform capable of sustained, localized therapeutic release within the female reproductive tract. This study investigates curcumin-loaded FBH as a novel topical therapeutic strategy for HPV-associated cervical cancer. We hypothesize that hydrogel-mediated delivery will enhance curcumin stability, local retention, and biological activity, resulting in improved antitumor efficacy and favorable modulation of the local immune microenvironment. To evaluate this approach, we will assess the effects of free and FBH-encapsulated curcumin in multiple HPV-positive cervical cancer cell lines. Antitumor activity will be characterized through measurements of cell viability, proliferation, apoptosis, and cytokine production to determine whether curcumin suppresses tumor growth and promotes immune activation. In parallel, we will investigate the immunological effects of curcumin in participants enrolled in an ongoing Phase I clinical study. Vaginal, rectal, and biopsy samples collected following curcumin treatment will be analyzed to evaluate drug absorption within squamous epithelial tissue and characterize local immune cell populations. Immune profiling will identify changes in markers of immune activation and immunosuppression associated with treatment and provide insight into the role of curcumin in promoting HPV clearance and disease control. Collectively, this work will establish foundational data on the antitumor and immunomodulatory potential of curcumin delivered through a biomaterial-based platform. By integrating in vitro studies with clinical immune profiling, this research seeks to advance a cost-effective, minimally invasive therapeutic strategy for HPV-associated cervical disease. Successful outcomes could support future clinical trials and contribute to reducing global disparities in cervical cancer treatment, particularly among underserved populations with limited access to conventional care. title: Changing landscape of oral squamous cell carcinoma: A scoping review of the pathogenesis, clinical profiles and prognosis of young, non‐smoking patients
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is traditionally associated with long-term exposure to tobacco and alcohol in older populations.However, a global epidemiological shift has revealed an increasing incidence among adults aged ≤45 years, many of whom lack canonical risk factors.The present scoping review aimed to evaluate the distinct clinicopathological, etiological and molecular landscape of young-onset OSCC, with a focus on emerging non-canonical drivers.For this purpose, a comprehensive synthesis of recent high-volume meta-analyses (encompassing >50,000 patients), genomic sequencing data and regional epidemiological reports from Central Asia and the Asia-Pacific was performed.The interplay between traditional carcinogens and novel factors, such as chronic mechanical irritation (CMI) and occupational hazards was analyzed.The analysis revealed a 'prognostic paradox': While younger patients faced a higher risk of local recurrence, their 5-year overall survival rate was superior or equivalent to that of older cohorts (hazard ratio, 0.97), likely due to greater physiological reserve and fewer comorbidities.Molecularly, young-onset OSCC in never-smokers and never-drinkers represents a distinct entity characterized by CDKN2A mutations, EGFR amplifications and a robust IFN-γ immune response, rather than human papillomavirus-driven oncogenesis.Furthermore, CMI functions as a potent 'effect modifier', lowering the threshold for malignant transformation through the TGF-β and NF-κB pathways.On the whole, the present scoping review indicates that the 'rejuvenation' of OSCC profiles mandates a shift from age-based to biology-driven risk stratification.Addressing non-canonical factors, such as dental trauma and occupational exposures is essential for early detection and functional preservation in this growing demographic.

title: Accelerating adoption of patient-centered cervical cancer screening and treatment linkage in Kenya: protocol for a cluster randomized effectiveness-implementation hybrid trial
abstract: Abstract Background Cervical Cancer (CC) is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women in Kenya. Despite effective screening and treatment methods, substantial gaps persist across the CC cascade, with low screening coverage and poor linkage to triage and treatment. These gaps reflect multi-level implementation barriers at the patient, provider, and health system levels. Effective and feasible strategies are needed to improve delivery of guideline-recommended CC services within routine primary care. Methods The DADA LINK study is a cluster randomized controlled trial evaluating implementation and effectiveness outcomes (type 2 hybrid) across 20 government primary healthcare facilities in Nairobi County, Kenya. Clinics are randomized 1:1 to receive either the DADA LINK care integration package or standard of care. The DADA LINK package integrates human papillomavirus (HPV) self-testing and patient support (technical assistance at clinics and an mHealth application, WEMA) to facilitate result notification and linkage to triage and treatment for women with positive HPV or visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA). Control clinics continue routine cervical cancer screening, referral, and treatment practices according to Kenyan National Guidelines. We will enroll 1,980 women aged 25–49 years presenting for care at Nairobi County clinics. Exclusion criteria include pregnancy, ≤ 6 weeks postpartum status, or known cervical cancer. The primary implementation outcome is completion of screening via either HPV self-testing or VIA. title: Abstract A043: Pacific Against Cervical Cancer (PACe) project: Implementation of a cervical cancer screening and treatment program in Yap, Federated States of Micronesia
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Cervical cancer incidence in the US-Affiliated Pacific Islands (USAPI) is among the highest in the world, with more than half of cases diagnosed at an advanced stage. Limited healthcare resources, geographic isolation, and sociocultural barriers reduce access to cervical cancer screening for many Pacific Islander women. To address these challenges, the Pacific Against Cervical Cancer (PACe) Project developed a locally tailored cervical cancer prevention program that piloted and translated a novel high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) self-collection screening approach for the island state of Yap, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). Methods: In partnership with the Yap State Department of Health Services, a multidisciplinary team—including experts in cervical cancer prevention and treatment, laboratory sciences, community engagement, and data systems—co-designed and implemented a community-engaged cervical cancer screening and treatment program across Yap's main island and 22 remote outer islands spanning more than 100,000 square miles of ocean. In addition to standard provider-collected screening for women aged 30-50 years, the program offered primary hrHPV self-collection screening and incorporated comprehensive capacity building through clinical and community health worker training. Screening was integrated with WHO-aligned visual assessment for treatment (VAT) and thermal ablation protocols to provide timely management of precancerous lesions. Results: Over a 4-year period, the PACe Project established local capacity by training 6 physicians and 5 nurses in cervical cancer screening and treatment, 16 community health workers in hrHPV education and motivational interviewing, and 15 clinic staff in the canSCREEN digital registry platform. The program expanded services to Yap's main island and 18 of its 22 outer islands, including atolls located more than 700 miles from the state capital. Screening exceeded the target goal of 1,600 women, reaching 1,892 women, of whom 86% chose hrHPV self-collection. The project also established electronic specimen tracking and local laboratory processing to improve continuity of care. 306 women tested positive for hrHPV (16% positivity rate), of which 87% completed VAT follow-up for evaluation and precancer treatment. 67% of the women screened had never been screened for cervical cancer. Conclusion: The PACe Project successfully implemented a locally tailored cervical cancer screening and treatment program in Yap, FSM, demonstrating that hrHPV self-collection can be effectively integrated into geographically dispersed, resource-limited island settings. Through community engagement, workforce development, and strengthened clinical infrastructure, the program substantially increased screening uptake and access to follow-up care. The implementation strategies developed in Yap, FSM through PACe provide a scalable model for expanding cervical cancer prevention, notably hrHPV screening with self-collection, across other USAPI jurisdictions and similarly rural and underserved populations in the U.S. Citation Format: Neal A. Palafox, Martina Reichhardt, James Edilyong, Kassandra Lelman, Mavis Nitta, Isabel Scarinci, Kathryn Maxwell, Enriquito Lu, Komal Soin, Rica Dela Cruz, Cerina Mariano, Emi Chutaro. title: Abstract A109: Birth cohort trends in cervical cancer incidence rates by race and ethnicity in the United States from 1929-1999
abstract: Abstract Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, introduced in the United States in 2006, has been associated with declines in cervical cancer incidence among young women, particularly among generations eligible for vaccination. However, national analyses can mask differences across racial and ethnic groups that vary in vaccination uptake, screening participation, and baseline cervical cancer risk. Therefore, we quantified birth cohort-specific cervical cancer incidence trends by race and ethnicity. Methods: We obtained annual invasive cervical cancer incidence data for women aged 20-79 years diagnosed from 2004-2023 across all 50 states and the District of Columbia from the U.S. Cancer Statistics Public Use Database. Analyses were stratified into five racial and ethnic groups: non-Hispanic White (NHW), non-Hispanic Black (NHB), non-Hispanic American Indian and Alaska Native (NH-AIAN), non-Hispanic Asian American or Pacific Islander (NH-AAPI), and Hispanic. For each group, rate matrices were constructed by 5-year age group and 5-year diagnosis period, yielding 15 overlapping 10-year birth cohorts, referenced by the mid-birth cohort year, from 1929 (1924-1933) through 1999 (1994-2003). Age-period-cohort models estimated fitted birth cohort-specific incidence rates at ages 30-34 years, adjusted for period deviations. Incidence rate ratios compared fitted rates for cohorts in the 1990s with those in the 1970s. Analyses were performed in MATLAB R2025b. Results: Fitted incidence rates among women aged 30-34 years declined across successive birth cohorts for most groups, with the largest reductions among NHB and NHW women. Between the 1970s and 1990s birth cohorts, incidence rates decreased from 9.5 to 3.5 per 100,000 population among NHB women, from 11.4 to 4.4 among NHW women, and from 11.7 to 6.1 among Hispanic women, corresponding to reductions of 63%, 62%, and 48%, respectively. Smaller nonsignificant reductions occurred among NH-AIAN women, from 14.9 to 10.1 per 100,000, and NH-AAPI women, from 4.7 to 3.7 per 100,000 women. Consequently, the ranking of racial and ethnic groups by incidence rates shifted across generations. Among women born in the 1990s, NHB women had the lowest fitted incidence rates, followed by NH-AAPI, NHW, Hispanic, and NH-AIAN. This reversed the pattern among women born in the 1930s, when Hispanic and NHB women had the highest incidence rates, followed by NH-AIAN, NHW, and NH-AAPI. Conclusions: Cervical cancer incidence declined substantially among recent birth cohorts across most races and ethnicities, but the magnitude of these declines varied. Differences in HPV vaccination uptake and screening participation likely influenced the varying birth cohort trajectories by race and ethnicity. Distinct birth cohort trajectories by race and ethnicity highlight opportunities for more tailored and targeted prevention efforts. Citation Format: Kieran Kelly, Chenxi Jiang, Angela Giaquinto, Philip Rosenberg, Ahmedin Jemal, Hyuna Sung. Birth cohort trends in cervical cancer incidence rates by race and ethnicity in the United States from 1929-1999 [abstract]. In: Proceedings of the 19th AACR Conference on the Science of Cancer Health Disparities; 2026 Oct 18-21; Atlanta, GA. Philadelphia (PA): AACR; Cancer Epidemiol Biomarkers Prev 2026;35(10 Suppl):Abstract nr A109.

title: Clinical Heterogeneity Across Oropharyngeal Cancer Datasets and Implications for Outcome Prediction
abstract: Importance Multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer datasets are increasingly used for research, yet systematic evaluation of data completeness and its clinical impact remains limited. Unrecognized institutional heterogeneity in variable availability, coding conventions, and patient characteristics can introduce substantial bias into combined analyses. Objective To systematically characterize data availability patterns and clinical heterogeneity across 2 major oropharyngeal cancer datasets, evaluate their impact on survival, and develop evidence-based recommendations for multi-institutional research design. Design, Setting, and Participants A cross-sectional analysis and retrospective cohort study was conducted of the RADCURE dataset (2005-2017) from Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (Toronto, Canada) and the HNSCC-Oropharyngeal dataset (2005-2012) from MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas). Patients with complete data on patient and disease characteristics were included. Data were analyzed from 2023 to 2026. Exposures Institutional dataset, human papillomavirus (HPV) status, tumor (T) stage, node (N) stage, harmonized treatment modality, smoking status, and age at diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures Data completeness rates across clinical and end point variables; overall survival assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis with Peto-Peto weighted log-rank tests, restricted mean survival time, and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression stratified by HPV status; machine learning discrimination and calibration for 1-, 5-, and 10-year survival prediction. Results The final analytic cohort comprised 1972 participants (median [IQR] age, 59.5 [53.4-67.0] years; 347 female [17.6%] and 1625 male [82.4%] individuals), 1482 from the RADCURE and 490 from the HNSCC-Oropharyngeal datasets. Of the total, 1263 had HPV-positive disease (64.0%). Substantial institutional differences were observed across demographic characteristics, HPV distribution, and treatment modality. After comprehensive adjustment, the hazard ratio for treating institutions was 1.19 (95% CI, 0.93-1.52), not excluding a clinically meaningful effect. HPV status violated the proportional hazards assumption, and its prognostic effect was quantified using restricted mean survival time, demonstrating a clinically meaningful survival advantage for patients with HPV-positive disease in both datasets. Machine learning ensemble models achieved moderate to good discrimination (1-year area under the curve [AUC], 0.820; 5-year AUC, 0.777; 10-year AUC 0.786) with institution consistently ranking as a low-importance predictor. Conclusions and Relevance In this cross-sectional analysis and cohort study, multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer datasets exhibited substantial heterogeneity requiring systematic harmonization prior to combined analyses. Systematic harmonization and rigorous assumption testing should be prerequisites for multi-institutional oropharyngeal cancer analyses; after appropriate adjustment, treating institution did not independently predict survival.

title: Abstract C168: Evaluating a community-engaged strategy to increase HPV vaccination access in rural communities
abstract: Abstract Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is associated with at least six types of cancer, yet many rural communities face persistent barriers to HPV vaccination, including limited healthcare access, transportation challenges, and fewer opportunities for preventive care. In response, the MUSC Hollings Cancer Center launched the HPV Vaccination Mobile Unit Program to expand access to evidence-based cancer prevention services in economically challenged regions. A key driver of the program’s success has been its commitment to meaningful community engagement. Guided by principles of collaboration, transparency, and sustainability, program leaders developed a multi-level partnership model involving school districts, local health departments, youth-serving organizations, and regional health coalitions. Through intentional outreach and co-developed implementation strategies, partners helped ensure mobile vaccination events aligned with local priorities and community needs. Long-term sustainability was prioritized from the outset. The program strengthened existing partnerships, expanded its network of collaborators, and implemented strategies to support continued service delivery. Sustainability efforts included integrating mobile vaccination clinics into annual school-based calendars, leveraging community health educators and school nurses as trusted advocates for HPV vaccination, maintaining existing funding streams, and securing additional sources of support. These efforts resulted in substantial and measurable growth. Over four years, the program expanded from 15 partners across 16 counties to 50 partners serving 31 counties, significantly increasing access to HPV vaccination in rural South Carolina. The program reached counties without pediatric healthcare providers, achieved strong engagement among rural and minority adolescents, and delivered services in communities with some of the state’s highest Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) scores. Participating counties experienced improvements in HPV vaccination uptake, while partner feedback highlighted increased trust, stronger collaboration, improved coordination of services, and greater awareness of HPV-related cancer prevention. This community-engaged model demonstrates a scalable and sustainable approach to reducing HPV vaccination disparities and advancing cancer prevention in rural and high-SVI communities. source_records.abstract: Abstract Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is associated with at least six types of cancer, yet many rural communities face persistent barriers to HPV vaccination, including limited healthcare access, transportation challenges, and fewer opportunities for preventive care. In response, the MUSC Hollings Cancer Center launched the HPV Vaccination Mobile Unit Program to expand access to evidence-based cancer prevention services in economically challenged regions. A key driver of the program’s success has been its commitment to meaningful community engagement. Guided by principles of collaboration, transparency, and sustainability, program leaders developed a multi-level partnership model involving school districts, local health departments, youth-serving organizations, and regional health coalitions. Through intentional outreach and co-developed implementation strategies, partners helped ensure mobile vaccination events aligned with local priorities and community needs. Long-term sustainability was prioritized from the outset. The program strengthened existing partnerships, expanded its network of collaborators, and implemented strategies to support continued service delivery. Sustainability efforts included integrating mobile vaccination clinics into annual school-based calendars, leveraging community health educators and school nurses as trusted advocates for HPV vaccination, maintaining existing funding streams, and securing additional sources of support. These efforts resulted in substantial and measurable growth. Over four years, the program expanded from 15 partners across 16 counties to 50 partners serving 31 counties, significantly increasing access to HPV vaccination in rural South Carolina. The program reached counties without pediatric healthcare providers, achieved strong engagement among rural and minority adolescents, and delivered services in communities with some of the state’s highest Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) scores. Participating counties experienced improvements in HPV vaccination uptake, while partner feedback highlighted increased trust, stronger collaboration, improved coordination of services, and greater awareness of HPV-related cancer prevention. This community-engaged model demonstrates a scalable and sustainable approach to reducing HPV vaccination disparities and advancing cancer prevention in rural and high-SVI communities. title: Abstract A119: Disparities in HPV-related cancer incidence by race and ethnicity and by disaggregated Asian American and Pacific Islander ethnicities in the United States, 2000-2022
abstract: Abstract Background: Persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection can cause cancers at six anatomic sites. In the United States, HPV infection prevalence and HPV-related cancer incidence varies by race and ethnicity, but analyses separating Asian and Pacific Islander populations have not been updated in over a decade. Using data through 2022, we compared HPV-related cancer incidence across racial and ethnic groups and by Asian American and Pacific Islander ethnicity. Methods: Incidence data (2000-2022) on HPV-related cancers [cervical carcinoma, vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), vaginal SCC, anal SCC, penile SCC, and oropharyngeal SCC] were obtained from two Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) databases. Non-Hispanic (NH) White, NH Black, NH American Indian/Alaska Native, and Hispanic data were obtained from SEER21. Detailed Asian and Pacific Islander data, including Asian ethnicity (Asian Indian/Pakistani, Chinese, Filipino, Japanese, Kampuchean, Korean, Laotian, and Vietnamese) and Pacific Islander ethnicity (Guamanian/CHamoru, Native Hawaiian, and Samoan) were obtained from the specialized SEER database. Age-standardized incidence rates (IRs) per 100,000 and IR ratios were calculated by race and ethnicity and by Asian and Pacific Islander ethnicity. Results: During 2000 to 2022, compared to Asian women, Pacific Islander women had higher IRs of cervical cancer [IR ratio=1.7, 95% confidence interval (95%CI)=1.6-1.8], and oropharyngeal (1.9, 95%CI=1.4-2.5), vulvar (2.1, 95%CI=1.5-2.8), and anal (2.5, 95%CI=1.8-3.4) SCC, but similar vaginal SCC IRs. Across all races, cervical cancer IRs ranged from 8.8 (Asian) to 14.9 (Hispanic and Pacific Islander); stratifying by Asian ethnicity revealed an even higher IR for Laotian women (15.8), which was 2.2 (95%CI=1.8-2.7) times that of Asian Indian/Pakistani women (7.2). By Pacific Islander ethnicity, cervical cancer incidence was highest for Samoan women (15.1) and was 1.9 (95%CI=1.2-3.2) times that of Guamanian/CHamoru women (8.0). Compared to Asian American men, Pacific Islander men had higher IRs of oropharyngeal (IR ratio=2.9, 95%CI=2.5-3.4), anal (2.9, 95%CI=1.9-4.2), and penile (1.6, 95%CI=1.0-2.4) SCC. Across all races, male oropharyngeal SCC IRs ranged from 2.3 (Asian) to 10.9 (NH White). By Asian ethnicity, male oropharyngeal SCC incidence was highest for Japanese men (3.6) and was 1.5 (95%CI=1.3-1.8) times that of Asian Indian/Pakistani men (2.5). By Pacific Islander ethnicity, male oropharyngeal SCC incidence was highest for Native Hawaiian men (7.8) and was 3.8 (95%CI=1.6-11.0) times that of Guamanian/CHamoru men (2.0). Conclusions: Our results emphasize the continued need to separate Asian from Pacific Islander population data in research. Further stratifying showed that some Asian and Pacific Islander ethnicities have disproportionately higher HPV-related cancer incidence, even surpassing the highest race-stratified rate. Identifying the underlying factors contributing to these racial and ethnic disparities are important for future HPV-related cancer prevention interventions. title: Abstract A099: Racial and ethnic differences in HPV-related second cancer risk among adult cancer survivors
abstract: Abstract Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the US. Cancer survivors face higher risk of developing an HPV-related second cancer, but research is limited on if these risks vary by race and ethnicity. Methods: Using 2000-2022 US Surveillance, Epidemiology and End Results 17 registries, we followed 7 million cancer survivors aged 20-89 years who survived ≥3 months. We calculated standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) for second HPV-related cancers [cervical cancer, and vulvar, vaginal, anal, oropharyngeal, and penile squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)] by race and ethnicity [Hispanic, non-Hispanic (NH) Asian American or Pacific Islander (AAPI), NH Black, and NH White] relative to race- and ethnic-matched general populations. P-heterogeneity tests compared SIRs across race and ethnicity. We calculated 10-year cumulative incidence after first cancer diagnosis. Results: In women, HPV-related second cancer risk relative to the general population varied by race and ethnicity for anal SCC after vulvar SCC (p=0.01), and vaginal SCC after cervical cancer (p=0.01). Notably, the relative risk of second anal SCC after vulvar SCC was high for Black women (SIR=38.2, 95%CI=17.4-72.5); relative risk of vaginal SCC after cervical carcinoma was high for AAPI women (SIR=101.5, 95%CI=64.3-152.3). In men, HPV-related second cancer risk relative to the general population varied by race and ethnicity for anal SCC after diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) (p<0.001), and oropharyngeal SCC after HPV-unrelated head and neck cancers (p<0.05). Notably, the relative risk of anal SCC after DLBCL was high for Black men (SIR=20.8, 95%CI=11.1-35.6). The relative risk of oropharyngeal SCC after oral cavity and pharynx cancer was high for AAPI men (SIR=22.2, 95%CI=12.2-37.3) and also after larynx cancer (SIR=19.1, 95%CI=9.1-35.1). For absolute risk in women, racial and ethnic differences occurred for cervical cancer after anal SCC: the 10-year cumulative incidence of cervical cancer after anal SCC was 0.9% (95%CI=0.4-1.9) in Black women vs 0.02% (95%CI=0.01-0.1) in White women. For absolute risk in men, 10-year cumulative incidences were generally similar by race and ethnicity. Conclusions: Among cancer survivors, relative and absolute risks of second HPV-related cancers by race and ethnicity differed. For survivors of cancers with HIV as a known risk factor, such as anal SCC and DLBCL, varying relative risks of second HPV-related cancer by race and ethnicity may reflect different HIV prevalences (e.g., higher HIV prevalence in Black populations). Similarly, for survivors of cancers with smoking as a risk factor, such as head and neck cancers, racial and ethnic differences in relative risks of second oropharyngeal SCC may reflect differences in smoking in the general population, while limited variation in absolute risk may reflect high smoking rates across all head and neck cancer survivors. title: Toll-like receptor expression across histological states of epidermodysplasia verruciformis
abstract: Abstract Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is characterized by susceptibility to cutaneous β -human papillomaviruses, persistent viral lesions, and an increased risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC). We investigated whether expression of Toll-like receptors 3, 4, 5, and 9 (TLR3, TLR4, TLR5, and TLR9) differs across histological states within EV. Immunoreactivity was quantified by digital H -score using QuPath in 97 specimens from 28 patients, comprising 13 lesion-free skin samples, 15 flat warts, and 69 cSCCs. Prespecified comparisons evaluated flat wart versus lesion-free skin, cSCC versus non-neoplastic tissue, and invasive versus in situ cSCC, with invasive tumor differentiation assessed secondarily. Patient-clustered generalized estimating equations and false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction were used for inference. After correction for multiple testing, TLR9 H -scores were higher in flat warts than in lesion-free skin ( β = 60.58; q = 0.0332). Compared with non-neoplastic tissue, cSCC showed lower TLR3 ( β = −81.40; q = 0.00745), higher TLR4 ( β = 55.59; q = 0.04793), and lower TLR9 expression ( β = −34.80; q = 0.03412). TLR5 showed a nominal increase in cSCC that did not meet the FDR threshold. None of the four receptors differed significantly between invasive and in situ cSCC, and no differentiation trend remained significant after FDR correction. These findings show receptor-specific differences in TLR expression across histological states of EV, particularly involving TLR3, TLR4, and TLR9, although the diagnostic and prognostic significance of these tissue patterns remains to be established.

title: Abstract B005: Machine learning-enhanced association analysis of ancestry-informative marker SNPs identifies predictors of head and neck cancer status in an underserved population
abstract: Abstract Background: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) exhibits persistent disparities in incidence, treatment, and survival among underserved populations. Although tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and human papillomavirus infection are established risk factors, inherited genetic variation also contributes to disease susceptibility. We investigated ancestry-informative marker (AIM) single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and supervised machine learning to identify genetic and clinical predictors of HNSCC. Methods: A retrospective case-control study included 905 participants (209 HNSCC cases, 696 controls). title: Abstract C002: Queer individuals' cervical cancer screening experiences
abstract: Abstract Purposes: This study aimed to describe queer individuals’ cervical cancer screening (CCS) experiences, examine how intersecting contextual factors across socioecological levels shape CCS experiences, and develop a participant-informed conceptualization of an affirming CCS experience. Background: In the United States, an estimated 13,490 invasive cervical cancers and 4,200 deaths will occur in 2026, yet 2023 CCS rates were only 75%. Sexual and gender minority people (SGMs) are more likely than straight or cisgender peers to never screen; just 68% of transgender men with a cervix are current; and lesbian, gay, bisexual, or queer women are 9% less likely to be up to date. Queer individuals experience persistent CCS disparities shaped by discrimination, gendered clinical environments, healthcare provider bias, medical mistrust, and cisnormative/heteronormative CCS protocols. Methods: We conducted a secondary qualitative descriptive analysis of interviews with 21 queer participants from 3 parent studies focused on CCS, high-risk human papillomavirus self-sampling for primary CCS, and cervical cancer prevention. Guided by the Social Ecological Model, queer theory, and the Minority Stress Model, 2 coders followed Creswell & Poth's iterative 6-step analytic process. A hybrid deductive-inductive approach used framework-derived codes to examine multilevel context, heteronormativity and cisnormativity, and distal and proximal minority stressors, while open coding preserved participant meanings. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus and analytic decisions documented. Results: Five themes characterized cross study synthesis: 1) clinical CCS as embodied vulnerability, 2) clinical spaces/climate and healthcare provider interactions as determinants of safety and trust, 3) minority stress shapes disclosure, expectations, and future CCS, 4) choice and control as foundations of affirming CCS, and 5) participant-defined affirming CCS pathways. Pain, exposure, dysphoria, nonaffirming assumptions, misgendering, and not being heard undermined trust; respectful language, consent, communication, and inclusive environments supported CCS. Among the subgroup offered CCS self-sampling; autonomy, privacy, and convenience were valued, although participants raised concerns about collection accuracy, discomfort, and result communication. Findings mirror prior evidence that provider and system experiences disproportionately shape SGMs’ screening behavior and extend evidence linking CCS to provider power, dysphoria, multilevel barriers, safety cues, navigation, and trauma-informed care. Conclusions: CCS inequities reflect interacting embodied, minority-stress, interpersonal, organizational, and structural conditions, not individual reluctance alone. Equity strategies should prioritize affirming clinical care; CCS self-sampling options; anatomy-based eligibility; tailored education; choice in CCS and results delivery; navigation; and reliable follow-up. This participant-defined framework offers actionable targets for multilevel intervention development and implementation. Citation Format: Mollie Aleshire, Ejemen Unuakhalu, Salsabeel Daraqel. title: Knowledge of oral cancer among Dental students and Dentists: A cross-sectional study
abstract: Oral cancer remains a major public health challenge due to its high morbidity and mortality, particularly when diagnosed at advanced stages. This study aimed to evaluate and compare oral cancer knowledge among undergraduate dental students and practicing dentists, identifying potential gaps in their theoretical knowledge and perceived clinical preparedness. An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted with 111 participants using a structured questionnaire addressing risk factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, and management of suspicious lesions. The overall knowledge score (0–10) was classified as low (≤6), moderate (7–8), or high (9–10). Associations were assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test, with a significance level of 5%. Most participants correctly identified tobacco use (97.3%), persistent painless ulcers (90.1%), and biopsy with histopathological examination (98.2%). However, knowledge gaps were identified regarding prognostic factors and the role of human papillomavirus in carcinogenesis. The mean knowledge score was 7.21 ± 1.43, with moderate knowledge predominating (59.5%). Higher educational level was significantly associated with better knowledge (p = 0.0024), while participation in training activities was associated with greater self-perceived preparedness to recognize suspicious lesions (p = 0.0014). These findings highlight the need to strengthen undergraduate education and continuing professional development to improve competencies in oral cancer prevention and early detection.

title: CÂNCER DO COLO DO ÚTERO: PREVENÇÃO E DIAGNÓSTICO PRECOCE NO BRASIL, DA VACINA HPV AO TESTE MOLECULAR
abstract: Introdução: O câncer do colo do útero, embora evitável por vacina, rastreamento e tratamento eficazes, é o terceiro mais incidente no Brasil (7,4%), com estimativa de mais de 19 mil novos casos anuais para 2026-2028. Em 2024, registrou 7.493 óbitos, com mortalidade no Norte duas vezes maior que no Sudeste e queda de 9 pontos na sobrevida em 5 anos (de 69,3% para 60,3%). A infecção persistente por HPV oncogênico (tipos 16 e 18) é a causa primária, agravada por tabagismo, multiparidade e imunossupressão. O SUS migra da citologia para o teste de DNA-HPV. O objetivo foi revisar a prevenção e o diagnóstico precoce no país. Método: Revisão na PubMed com descritores como Neoplasias do Colo do Útero e Vacinas contra Papillomavirus, selecionando 21 artigos adequados aos objetivos, sintetizados conforme a literatura vigente . Resultados e discussão: A prevenção primária fundamenta-se na vacinação de meninos e meninas de 9 a 14 anos, em dose única, e na educação sexual com preservativos, sendo a falta de conhecimento apontada por revisão sistemática brasileira como principal barreira vacinal. Na secundária, a citologia vigorou até 2025, ano em que o Ministério da Saúde iniciou a implantação do teste de DNA-HPV para mulheres de 25 a 64 anos a cada 5 anos, por profissional ou autocoleta. O método antecipa a detecção pré-citológica e amplia o acesso, sendo recomendado pela OMS (2021) como preferencial, amparado por análise de ensaios europeus que demonstra proteção de 60% a 70% superior contra carcinoma invasivo frente à citologia. Resultados alterados conduzem à colposcopia com biópsia dirigida: lesões de baixo grau (NIC 1), propensas à regressão, recebem seguimento, enquanto as de alto grau (NIC 2 e 3) são manejadas por excisão da zona de transformação (CAF). O acompanhamento ocorre em 6 e 12 meses, garantindo alta e retorno à rotina com dois exames consecutivos normais. Sinais como sangramentos anormais (pós-coito, intermenstrual ou pós-menopáusico), corrimento persistente e dor pélvica exigem exame especular e encaminhamen

title: Beyond Viral Suppression: Persistent HPV-Associated Cancer Risk in People With HIV
abstract: In the past 2 decades, a central tenet of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-associated oncology has been that viral suppression, and the immune restoration that follows, reduces the excess cancer risk driven by HIV for certain malignancies. This has been the case for cancers caused by oncogenic viruses, which were historically termed “acquired immunodeficiency syndrome-defining cancers” and include Kaposi sarcoma and subtypes of non-Hodgkin lymphomas, whose incidence has fallen significantly in the antiretroviral therapy (ART) era [1]. Cancers caused by human papillomavirus (HPV), however, have been persistent in the modern ART era [2, 3]. Cervical cancer incidence has changed little relative to the general population [4], and the risk of cancers of the anus, penis, and vulva remains elevated and, in some settings, continues to increase [5–7]. This observed difference between incidence of virus-associated cancers that recede with immune reconstitution and those that do not raises a fundamental question: can HPV-related oncogenesis be reversed with ART, or are control of HIV and prevention of HPV-associated malignancies distinct objectives? In the accompanying study, Mendu and colleagues address this question in Botswana, a country with high burden of both HIV and HPV-associated cancer [8, 9]. The investigators use 2 large population-based cohorts; first is a prospective cancer cohort and, second, is a random community sample from the Ya Tsie HIV prevention trial. Botswana has a mature public ART program with near universal coverage, which permits evaluation across a range of treatment durations. Applying a case-cohort design, the investigators emulate a target trial to estimate how anogenital cancer risk changes with increasing duration of ART. The study included 4 major HPV-associated anogenital malignancies, impacting both women and men, and differing in their incidence and availability of preventative measures. In the setting of widespread ART coverage and viral suppression (98% below 1000 copies/mL among 80% with an available measurement), the relative risk of cervical, anal, vulvar, and penile cancer did not decline with longer treatment. Rather, among people with HIV (PWH) receiving ART for a decade or more, the marginal relative risk of anogenital cancer was 7-fold higher than that of people without HIV, with even higher estimates for penile and vulvar cancers. Importantly, duration of ART and duration of HIV infection were nearly identical in this population. Additionally, those with longer ART duration had a history of advanced HIV disease, reflecting CD4+ T cell–based criteria used to initiate treatment in the earlier years of the HIV epidemic. The findings highlight that control of HIV replication and prevention of HPV-associated anogenital cancers are not interchangeable outcomes. Few studies have evaluated long-term cancer outcomes in treated HIV populations with comparable methodological rigor. The findings should not be interpreted as evidence that ART lacks anticancer benefit or promotes carcinogenesis. In fact, recent observational studies and long-term follow-up from randomized trials suggest that earlier ART initiation reduces subsequent malignancy risk [10–12], although neither the ATHENA nor START studies focused on HPV-associated anogenital cancers alone. One explanation is that the biologic window during which ART most influences cancer risk occurs early in HIV infection, before persistent immune dysfunction and HPV-mediated carcinogenesis are fully established. The study by Mendu and colleagues was not designed to test that hypothesis because it compared duration of ART rather than timing of ART initiation relative to HIV acquisition. In the study population, duration of ART functions as a marker of cumulative HIV infection, rather than as an independent exposure. Furthermore, the long latency of HPV-mediated carcinogenesis is central to the interpretation of the study findings. HPV-associated cancer development spans years to decades. HPV infection can precede ART initiation or occur during periods of uncontrolled infection [13]. In spite of immune reconstitution, there may be incomplete restoration of antitumor surveillance or reversal of oncogenic processes already under way. Persistent immune activation, immune senescence, inflammaging, and altered tissue microenvironments have all emerged as plausible mechanisms linking treated HIV infection to ongoing cancer risk [14–17]. The a priori definition of advanced HIV disease used in the study, which included a World Health Organization stage 3 or 4 illness and nadir CD4+ T-cell count <250 cells/μL, were developed to predict opportunistic infections and guide ART initiation, not to stratify cancer risk. If persistent cancer risk reflects multiple biologic pathways, prevention must also be multifaceted. HPV vaccination, smoking cessation, and prompt ART initiation remain essential, but they address only part of the process of HPV-associated cancer development. Screening and treatment of precancerous lesions provide an independent opportunity to interrupt progression to invasive cancer. The ANCHOR trial demonstrated that treatment of anal high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions reduces progression to anal cancer in PWH, establishing proof that secondary prevention can reduce cancer incidence in PWH [18]. Whether similar strategies can be successfully implemented in global low-resource settings remains uncertain. In the present study, the more modest increase in cervical cancer risk compared to anal, vulvar, and penile cancers may reflect Botswana's longstanding national cervical screening program [19], again highlighting the impact of secondary prevention. Reducing the burden of HPV-associated cancers will require multidisciplinary integration of prevention, screening, timely diagnosis, cancer treatment, and survivorship care. The study findings highlight future opportunities for cancer biology and implementation science to shape prevention efforts. Biomarkers beyond CD4+ T-cell count and viral load are needed to better characterize persistent immune dysfunction, improve cancer risk stratification, and identify new drug targets. On the implementation side, effective prevention strategies, such as anal cancer screening, need to be scaled to reach the populations most likely to benefit. ART has transformed outcomes for PWH; extending that success to cancer prevention will require a deeper understanding of why cancer risk persists despite viral suppression. Viral suppression remains the foundation of HIV care, but it should not be regarded as the final measure of long-term success. As PWH age, the challenge shifts from controlling infection to preventing its chronic sequelae, among the most consequential of which are HPV-associated malignancies. The work of Mendu and colleagues reminds us that successful HIV treatment and successful cancer prevention are related but distinct goals. Achieving both will require continued advances in our understanding of determinants of persistent cancer risk and integration of that knowledge into prevention strategies, clinical guidelines, and comprehensive HIV care. receives funding from the National Institutes of Health/National Cancer Institute/NCI and ARPA-H that are unrelated to this manuscript.

title: Standardized country-level delivery unit cost estimates for routine childhood, routine adolescent, and campaign vaccination: an updated modeling analysis
abstract: Background: Reliable estimates of immunization delivery costs are essential for planning, budgeting, and economic evaluation. Despite recent empirical studies, many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) lack up-to-date cost estimates, particularly for adolescent and campaign vaccination. This study generated standardized country-level delivery cost estimates across vaccination modalities in LMICs. Methods: Using data from empirical costing studies in the 2024 update of the Immunization Delivery Cost Catalogue, we fitted Bayesian meta-regression models to estimate per-dose delivery costs, not including vaccine and injection supplies costs, for routine childhood vaccination, routine adolescent vaccination (using human papillomavirus vaccination as a proxy), and mass campaigns. Models incorporated country-level covariates (gross domestic product per capita, population size, diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis third-dose coverage, urbanization, population density, and under-five mortality) and study-level characteristics (cost category and costing perspective). Fitted models were used to generate country-specific and population-weighted mean economic and financial costs per dose in 2024 US dollars. Results: The analysis included 141 observations for routine childhood, 49 for adolescent, and 104 for campaign vaccination. The population-weighted mean full economic cost per dose across LMICs was $4.27 (95% prediction interval: $1.95-11.58) for routine childhood vaccination, $20.56 ($8.56-57.83) for adolescent vaccination, and $14.71 ($4.90-86.98) for campaigns. Corresponding estimates for incremental economic costs per dose were $16.64 ($7.90-38.22), $20.43($8.27-47.78), and $3.53 ($1.70-8.56). Substantial heterogeneity was observed across countries, delivery modalities, and cost perspectives. Conclusions: Leveraging an expanded evidence-base and Bayesian meta-regression, this study provides updated delivery cost estimates across vaccination modalities for 136 LMICs. These estimates offer a practical resource for analyses where empirical cost data are unavailable.
